0.title: A Farewell Letter from the Rock
0.overview:
The message. Second Peter is the apostle’s farewell letter. He writes knowing that he will soon die: “the putting off of my body will be soon, as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me” (1:14; compare John 21:18–19). False teachers have crept into the churches. They twist Paul’s letters, live immorally, and argue that because the world has always gone on as it is, Christ will never return. Peter’s answer is to remind his readers of what they already have and what is surely coming: God’s power has given them “all things that pertain to life and godliness” (1:3), the word of the apostles and prophets is sure, and the day of the Lord will come. So they are to grow, to stand firm, and to live now as people who expect Christ.

Background: the writer. The letter names its author as “Simeon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ” (1:1), using the Hebrew form of his name. Peter, the fisherman who once denied his Lord and was restored, now writes near the end of his life. He was probably in Rome, about AD 64–68, and early tradition holds that he was crucified there under Nero. The letter is a last testament, like Moses’ farewell in Deuteronomy or Paul’s in 2 Timothy: Peter calls his death his “departure” (1:15), the word Luke uses for what Jesus would accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31), and he means to leave a written reminder that will outlast him (1:12–15).

The first readers. Peter calls this his second letter to the same people (3:1), most likely the mainly Gentile churches of the five provinces of Asia Minor addressed in 1 Peter. The danger has changed. In the first letter it came from outside, as a hostile society slandered and shut out believers; now it comes from inside, from teachers who sit at the church’s own feasts (2:13). They promise “freedom” (2:19) while serving their appetites, they exploit the flock for money (2:3, 14), and they scoff at the promise of Christ’s coming (3:3–4). Their outlook resembles ideas common in the Greek world, where some philosophers taught that the gods do not intervene and that there is no judgment to fear. Peter even borrows a Greek word his readers knew, Tartarus, for the place where the rebel angels are held (2:4).

Did Peter really write it? No New Testament book has had its authorship questioned more. Origen and Eusebius record that some in the early church doubted it, and its style differs sharply from 1 Peter. Most modern scholars think a follower wrote it in Peter’s name after his death, pointing to that difference of style, to its heavy use of Jude, to its counting Paul’s letters with “the other Scriptures” (3:16), and to the remark that “the fathers fell asleep” (3:4). These are real questions, but the letter identifies its author in unusual detail: the name Simeon Peter, an eyewitness account of the Transfiguration (1:16–18), Jesus’ prediction of his death (1:14), and an earlier letter (3:1). The early church rejected writings it knew to be falsely attributed, and after careful weighing it received this one. The difference of style is well explained by a different secretary, or none (Silvanus helped with 1 Peter, 1 Peter 5:12), and by a different subject. The question cannot be settled by proof either way; this commentary receives the letter as Peter’s, as the church long has, and as Scripture.

Peter and Jude. Chapter 2 shares much with the letter of Jude: the angels who sinned, Sodom and Gomorrah, Balaam, the waterless springs and storm-driven mists, the scoffers of the last days. Most scholars think Peter knew Jude’s letter and adapted it, and that is the more likely reading. Peter does not merely copy: he omits Jude’s references to writings outside the Old Testament, adds the rescue of Noah and Lot, and turns the warning toward the hope of Christ’s return, which these teachers attacked.

How the letter makes its case. The three chapters answer three dangers. Chapter 1 answers careless living. God has already given everything needed, and by his promises believers become “partakers of the divine nature” (1:4), sharing his holiness, not his being. On that gift rests the command to add to faith a chain of virtues ending in love, and so to confirm their calling (1:5–11). Gift first, then effort: that is the order grace always follows. Peter then grounds the message in two witnesses that agree: “we did not follow cleverly devised myths” but were “eyewitnesses of his majesty” on the holy mountain (1:16), and the prophetic word, spoken by men “carried along by the Holy Spirit” (1:21), shines like “a lamp shining in a dark place” (1:19). Chapter 2 answers the teachers who corrupt the faith. It portrays their method (slipping in quietly), their doctrine (denying their Master), their motive (greed), and their end: judgment already on its way (2:1–3). The angels, the flood and Sodom show that God judges the wicked, and Noah and Lot that “the Lord knows how to rescue the godly” (2:9). The test of a teacher is not how clever his words are but how he lives. Chapter 3 answers the mockers of Christ’s return. The world has not always gone on as it was: God’s word made it and judged it by water, and by the same word it is kept for fire (3:5–7). God is not slow but patient, “not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance” (3:9). And the day will come like a thief, laying everything bare (3:10). So the question is not “When?” but “what sort of people ought you to be” (3:11)?

Where it leads: to Christ. From its greeting the letter calls Jesus “our God and Savior Jesus Christ” (1:1), and it ends, unusually, with a doxology to the Son: “To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity” (3:18). The Transfiguration Peter saw was a preview of the coming he defends: the same Lord who shone on the mountain will appear in glory. The false teachers deny “the Master who bought them” (2:1); the true believer belongs to him by purchase. The God who kept Noah through the flood and brought Lot out of Sodom rescues his people still, and the patience that delays the end is the patience of Christ, given for salvation (3:15). The day that dissolves the present order brings “new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells” (3:13), this creation purged and renewed under its rightful King.

For us. Second Peter is for churches tempted to live as though Christ were not coming: drifting, tolerating teachers who make sin comfortable, or quietly assuming with the scoffers that tomorrow will be like today. It tells you that you already have what you need for godliness, that the Scriptures are a sure lamp in a dark place, and that every day of delay is mercy, a day for repentance and the gospel. It asks you not to calculate dates but to be found “without spot or blemish, and at peace” (3:14). Its last command is its first concern: “grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” (3:18).

1.title: Partakers of the Divine Nature
1.text: <sup>1</sup>Simeon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, To those who have obtained a faith of equal standing with ours by the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ:<sup>2</sup>May grace and peace be multiplied to you in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord.<sup>3</sup>His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us to his own glory and excellence,<sup>4</sup>by which he has granted to us his precious and very great promises, so that through them you may become partakers of the divine nature, having escaped from the corruption that is in the world because of sinful desire.<sup>5</sup>For this very reason, make every effort to supplement your faith with virtue, and virtue with knowledge,<sup>6</sup>and knowledge with self-control, and self-control with steadfastness, and steadfastness with godliness,<sup>7</sup>and godliness with brotherly affection, and Christ.<sup>9</sup>For whoever lacks these qualities is so nearsighted that he is blind, having forgotten that he was cleansed from his former sins.<sup>10</sup>Therefore, brothers, be all the more kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.<sup>12</sup>Therefore I intend always to remind you of these qualities, though you know them and are established in the truth that you have.<sup>13</sup>I think it right, as long as I am in this body, to stir you up by way of reminder,<sup>14</sup>since I know that the putting off of my body will be soon, as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me.<sup>15</sup>And I will make every effort so that after my departure you may be able at any time to recall these things.<sup>16</sup>For we did not follow cleverly devised myths when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty.<sup>17</sup>For when he received honor and glory from God the Father, and the voice was borne to him by we have the prophetic word more fully confirmed, to which you will do well to pay attention as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your 1.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 opens Peter’s farewell letter. Before he exposes the false teachers (chapter 2) and answers the scoffers who mock Christ’s return (chapter 3), he lays the foundation his readers will stand on.

The message. You already have everything you need in Christ, so grow, and do not let anyone move you off the truth you were given. God’s power has granted his people all that life and godliness require, and by his promises they share his own holy character. That gift is the reason for effort, not a substitute for it: add to your faith, all the way to love, and you will be sure of your calling and richly welcomed into Christ’s kingdom. And the message you believed is no clever story: the apostles saw Christ’s glory with their own eyes, and the Scriptures that point to him came from God.

Why it was said. Peter knows he will soon die (v. 14), and teachers inside the churches are offering a “knowledge” that frees people from ordinary holiness and laughs at the promise of Christ’s coming (see the introduction). So he writes a last testament: a reminder meant to outlast him (vv. 12–15).

How the chapter makes its case. The greeting sets the tone: every believer’s faith is as precious as an apostle’s, because it rests on the righteousness of “our God and Savior Jesus Christ” (vv. 1–2). Then the gift: divine power, precious promises, a share in God’s nature (vv. 3–4). Then the response: a chain of qualities running from faith to love (vv. 5–7), whose presence keeps knowledge fruitful and whose absence is a kind of blindness that has forgotten its cleansing (vv. 8–9), and by which believers make their calling sure (vv. 10–11). Gift first, then effort: that is the order grace always follows. The second half explains why Peter keeps repeating himself (vv. 12–15) and grounds the message in two witnesses that agree: the apostles on the holy mountain, who saw the majesty Christ will have when he comes (vv. 16–18), and the prophetic word, spoken by men carried along by the Holy Spirit and shining like a lamp until the day dawns (vv. 19–21).

Where it leads. The whole chapter hangs on a person. We share the divine nature only because the Son first shared ours. Every quality in the chain was first seen in him. The voice on the mountain called him “my beloved Son”, and the morning star the lamp is waiting for is Christ himself, coming in the glory three fishermen glimpsed for a moment.

For us. If you feel second-class, stalled, or unsure whether the Christian story is true, this chapter answers all three. Your faith is as precious as Peter’s; you lack no resource, only growth in using it; and the gospel rests on what was seen, heard and written by God’s Spirit. So keep the lamp near, and keep growing until the day dawns.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Divine Power and Precious Promises
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God has given his people everything they need, so they must put everything into growing. Peter greets believers whose faith is as precious as his own, because it rests on the righteousness of Jesus, our God and Saviour (vv. 1–2). God’s power has granted all that life and godliness require, and his promises give a share in his holy nature (vv. 3–4). On that gift rests the command to add to faith a chain of qualities ending in love (vv. 5–7). Where they grow, knowledge bears fruit; where they are missing, a believer has forgotten his cleansing (vv. 8–9). And by them believers make their calling sure, and are promised a rich welcome into Christ’s eternal kingdom (vv. 10–11).
verseByVerse.theology:
Partakers of the Divine Nature

God’s power has already granted everything needed for life and godliness. Sharing the divine nature means sharing his holiness, not becoming God, and growth in the qualities of verses 5–7 is how a believer confirms his calling.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter told readers who had seen nothing that their faith was of equal standing with his.

Now: When growth stalls, look first for a memory of forgiveness that has grown dim (v. 9).

verseByVerse.quote: Simeon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, To those who have obtained a faith of equal standing with ours by the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ: May grace and peace be multiplied to you in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter, near the end of his life, greets believers whose faith is worth exactly as much as an apostle’s, because it rests on the righteousness of Jesus Christ, our God and Saviour. And he prays that their grace and peace will grow as they come to know God and Jesus better.

Simeon Peter. Not Simon but Symeōn, the old Hebrew form (some manuscripts, and the KJV, read Simon), used of Peter elsewhere only by James (Acts 15:14). Then the name Jesus gave him, Petros, rock. Signing his last letter, he signs his whole history: the fisherman who sank in the lake and swore he did not know the man, and the rock he never became by his own strength but was made by the One who named him.

A servant and apostle. Servant first, doulos, a slave, and apostle second. The man who once argued about who was the greatest now introduces himself as the property of another. As Christ’s slave he speaks with Christ’s authority, carrying a message that is not his own and in which he has no ambitions of his own.

A faith of equal standing. Obtained, lachousin, is a word for receiving by lot: faith is a gift, not a prize won (Ephesians 2:8). Of equal standing, isotimon, means of the same value. Peter saw the Transfiguration and will describe it in fifteen verses; he tells readers who have seen nothing, mostly Gentiles who never heard Jesus’ voice, that their faith is worth exactly as much as his. There is no first-class and second-class Christianity.

By the righteousness. Righteousness, dikaiosynē, carries two shades together: God’s fairness in giving the same faith to all, Jew and Gentile, apostle and newcomer; and the righteousness of Christ himself, credited to the one who trusts him, by which God counts him righteous (Romans 4:5). The faith is equal because the righteousness is Christ’s, and it is not divided into larger and smaller portions.

Our God and Savior Jesus Christ. In Greek one “the” covers both titles, which normally marks them as one person. Peter calls Jesus God directly, as Paul does in Titus 2:13, and the same construction in 1:11, 2:20 and 3:18 (“our Lord and Savior”) plainly names one person. It is among the New Testament’s clearest statements of Christ’s deity, set at the front door of a letter against men who denied the Master who bought them (2:1). The fisherman who once denied him calls himself his slave and calls him God in the same breath, and is glad to do both.

Grace and peace be multiplied. Not merely given but multiplied (1 Peter 1:2), for the God who gives grace never runs short of it. Grace is his free favour; peace is what it produces: reconciliation with God and rest within.

In the knowledge of God. The letter’s key word: epignōsis, full, personal knowledge, the knowing that belongs to a relationship rather than a library (1:2, 3, 8; 2:20). The false teachers were probably offering knowledge of another kind: secret, superior, freeing people from ordinary morality. Peter answers not by despising knowledge but by naming the true knowledge of God in Christ.

The setting. The first letter was written to Christians suffering from outside; this one to Christians endangered from inside, by teachers who denied Christ’s return and lived immorally (chapters 2–3; see the introduction). Persecution can kill the body, but false teaching can empty a church while leaving its building full, and Peter, with the executioner not far off, judged it the greater danger.

What it does not mean. “Equal standing” does not mean all believers share the apostles’ authority. It means the same saving faith, equally precious to God: equality of faith, not of office (3:2).

In everyday life. If you know someone who feels like a second-class believer, the new convert with a chaotic past, the believer who cannot pray aloud, tell them what Peter told his readers: your faith is as precious as his.

My faith feels nothing like an apostle’s. How can it be equal? Because faith is valued not by its strength but by the one it trusts. A trembling hand and a strong one receive the same gift, and a weak faith in a mighty Christ saves as surely as a bold one. Thomas, who doubted, and the thief, who believed in his last hours, received the same Saviour as Peter. So do not measure your standing by comparing your faith with other people’s. Measure it by whom you are trusting, and grow from there.

Is this knowledge just a matter of learning doctrine? Never less than that: you cannot know a person while being wrong about who he is. But Peter means knowing God as a child knows his father, trusting and walking with him over years, through his word, prayer, his people, and obeying him and finding him faithful. A man can know a great deal about God and not know him; a simple believer may know little theology and know him truly. The aim is both.

Textual note. 2 Peter was among the most disputed books in the early church. Most modern scholars think a follower wrote it in Peter’s name after his death, pointing to its style, unlike 1 Peter’s, its heavy use of Jude, its counting Paul’s letters with the Scriptures (3:15–16), and the remark that the fathers have fallen asleep (3:4). On the other side, the letter plainly claims to be Peter’s, speaks as an eyewitness of the Transfiguration (vv. 16–18), and recalls Jesus’ prediction of Peter’s death (v. 14) and a previous letter (3:1); the early church, which rejected writings it knew to be falsely attributed, received this one after careful weighing; and a different secretary or none (Silvanus helped with 1 Peter, 1 Peter 5:12), and a different subject, may explain the style. Honest scholars weigh this differently, and proof is not possible either way (see the introduction). This commentary receives the letter as Peter’s, as the church long has, and as Scripture.
verseByVerse.note: Peter’s farewell letter, written as he expected to die soon (1:14), probably from Rome in the mid 60s AD. “Simeon” is the Hebrew form of his name.

verseByVerse.quote: His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us to his own glory and excellence, by which he has granted to us his precious and very great promises, so that through them you may become partakers of the divine nature, having escaped from the corruption that is in the world because of sinful desire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has already given his people everything they need to live for him, and through his promises they come to share his own holy character, having fled the rot of a world driven by desire.

His divine power has granted. Granted, dedōrēmenēs, is perfect tense: given, and still ours. Not supplied in instalments, but given in full. The sentence shuts the false teachers’ door in advance: if everything necessary has been provided, anyone promising a further instalment is selling what does not exist.

Him who called us. Called, kalesantos, is the call of God that brings about the response it asks for, as Jesus’ voice brought Lazarus out of the tomb.

His own glory and excellence. Glory, doxa, is the radiance of who he is. Excellence, aretē, is moral goodness, the word Peter uses for “the excellencies of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light” (1 Peter 2:9). He calls us into the very thing he is (see “Uncertain wording” below).

Precious and very great promises. Precious, timia, is Peter’s recurring word (1 Peter 1:7, 19). The promises include forgiveness, the Spirit, eternal life, Christ’s return, and the new heavens and new earth in which righteousness dwells (3:4, 9, 13). They are given, not dangled: God has bound himself by his word, and every one of his promises finds its Yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20).

Partakers of the divine nature. Partakers, koinōnoi, is the word for business partners in Luke 5:10, where James and John were Simon’s partners in the fishing. Through his promises believers share God’s own moral character and life, his holiness, love and goodness, by the new birth and union with Christ (John 15:4–5; Colossians 3:10). Not that we become God (see below), yet it is no exaggeration: the Spirit lives in every believer (Romans 8:9), giving desires that are God’s own, to love what he loves and hate what he hates. You remain a creature, but you are no longer only what you were.

Having escaped from the corruption. Escaped, apophygontes, means fled, as from a burning building. Corruption, phthora, is moral rot, and the world’s rot comes from disordered desire (James 1:14–15). By naming its opposite, the clause shows that sharing the divine nature means sharing God’s holiness, not becoming divine. The false teachers, Peter will say, promise freedom while they are slaves of this same corruption (2:19). There are only two directions, toward God’s life or toward the rot, and he has brought us out of the one into the other.

He shared ours. The way into this sharing runs through the incarnation. Since the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same things, that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death (Hebrews 2:14). The Son took our nature without ceasing to be God, so that in union with him we might receive his life without ceasing to be creatures. We share the divine nature only because the divine Son first, and freely, shared the human one.

The oldest upgrade. Our culture promises to make us more than we are: hack your biology, become the best version of yourself, even upgrade humanity beyond its limits. The longing is very old. In the garden the serpent offered exactly this: “you will be like God” (Genesis 3:5). He was right that we were made for more, and wrong about the route: reaching up and taking it on our own terms. Every self-improvement project, religious or secular, runs on that engine, and ends in pride or exhaustion. Peter announces the reversal: what Adam grasped at, God gives, because the Son came down, who did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped but emptied himself (Philippians 2:6–7). We do not become gods; by grace we become like him, which is far better.

In everyday life. Carry one promise of God through the day. Anxious? He will never leave you (Hebrews 13:5). Tempted? He provides a way of escape (1 Corinthians 10:13). Guilty? He forgives the one who confesses (1 John 1:9). When the desire that rots presses on you, answer it with what God has said.

If I have everything, why do I feel I am lacking so much? Because having and using are different things. A man may inherit a great house and live cold and hungry in one room of it, never opening the other doors. Peter does not say you feel complete; he says the resources are yours, and what you lack is growth in using them, which is why the next verses call for effort. So when someone offers a secret, a second blessing or an experience that will finally make the Christian life work, answer kindly: I have all things in Christ; I need to know him better, not something besides him.

How can a promise make me share God’s nature? Because God’s promises are not information about a distant future but the means by which the Spirit unites us to Christ now. Believe that your sins are forgiven, and you are freed from guilt and drawn to love him. Believe that Christ is coming and you will be like him, and you begin to purify yourself as he is pure (1 John 3:2–3). A promise believed changes what you want, until his character is reproduced in yours.

Where Christians differ: do believers become divine? Eastern Orthodoxy teaches theosis or deification, in which believers progressively become gods by grace; Orthodox theologians themselves insist that believers share God’s energies, his life and activity, never his essence, so the difference from Reformed teaching is real but narrower than it sounds. Some modern movements go further and teach that believers become little gods. This commentary’s view: believers share in God’s moral nature (his holiness, love and life) through union with Christ by the Spirit, but never in his essence, his deity, or incommunicable attributes such as omnipotence or omniscience. The Creator-creature distinction is never erased. We become like God in character, not God in being (1 John 3:2; 2 Corinthians 3:18).

Uncertain wording. “Called us to his own glory and excellence” can also be translated “by his own glory and excellence”. If “by”, God drew us through the display of his beauty and goodness, as Peter was drawn when he fell at Jesus’ knees in the boat (Luke 5:8); if “to”, he called us to share them. Both are true, and Peter may intend both.

verseByVerse.quote: For this very reason, make every effort to supplement your faith with virtue, and virtue with knowledge, and knowledge with self-control, and self-control with steadfastness, and steadfastness with godliness, and godliness with brotherly affection, and brotherly affection with love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because God has given you everything, put all your energy into growing, adding to your faith a family of Christlike qualities that reaches its crown in love.

For this very reason, make every effort. Because God has given you everything (vv. 3–4). Make every effort, spoudēn pasan pareisenenkantes, is literally bringing in all diligence alongside: God has brought everything; you bring your diligence beside it. Grace is opposed not to effort but to earning (Philippians 2:12–13). A man given a farm does not earn it by ploughing, but he will certainly plough.

Supplement your faith with virtue. Supplement comes from the wealthy citizen who paid lavishly for a festival chorus (epichorēgēsate, from chorēgos; compare 1 Peter 4:11). Eight qualities follow in a chain, beginning with faith, each growing out of the one before. The first is virtue, aretē, moral excellence, the word used of God in verse 3.

Knowledge. Here understanding and practical wisdom (gnōsis): knowing God’s will and how to apply it. Goodness without understanding blunders (Romans 10:2).

Self-control. Literally holding oneself in (enkrateia). Knowing what is right settles nothing until the appetites are governed. The false teachers claimed knowledge without self-control (2:10–14), and Peter shows where that ends.

Steadfastness. Endurance, remaining under weight (hypomonē; James 1:3–4): self-control extended over time. Anyone can resist a temptation once. Steadfastness resists it on the four hundredth day, when the novelty of the fight has gone and the pressure has not.

Godliness. Reverence for God shown in life (eusebeia). A pagan philosopher could have admired the qualities so far; godliness makes them Christian: everything done before God’s face, for his sake.

Brotherly affection. Family love for fellow believers (philadelphia): warmth, loyalty, enjoyment of one another as children of one Father. Godliness that does not love God’s children is not godliness (1 John 4:20).

Love. Love (agapē), set beyond brotherly affection, is the self-giving love that reaches past the family to everyone, enemies included, the crown of the list (1 Corinthians 13:13; Colossians 3:14). It is the link that looks most like Christ, who loved his own and prayed for those who crucified him.

Every link was first in Christ. The chain is a portrait: faith resting wholly on the Father, goodness without a stain, knowledge of the Father’s will so perfect that he always did what pleased him, self-control in the wilderness when he was hungry, steadfastness all the way to the cross, godliness that said “not my will, but yours, be done”, affection for his brothers, and love for his enemies. The God who called us by that excellence will reproduce it in us, until the family likeness is complete.

In everyday life. Ask someone who knows you well which link they see missing in you, and then be specific: not “I will be more loving”, but “I will visit, phone or help this person, whom I have been avoiding.”

Is this effort not a kind of legalism? No. Legalism is effort to earn God’s favour or add to Christ’s work; Peter’s effort springs from favour already given. A slave labouring to buy his freedom and a son working in his father’s fields may both sweat, but only one does it from rest. If your effort has become anxious, proud or joyless, do not stop trying; go back to verses 3–4. And lest the list become a project for admiring yourself, Peter’s chain is guarded at both ends: it begins with faith, which only receives, and ends with love, which gives itself away.

Must I master these qualities one at a time, in order? No. This is not a staircase where you finish one step before the next. The links grow together, like branches on one tree; the order shows how they depend on one another (knowledge guides goodness, self-control keeps knowledge honest, endurance makes self-control last). A young believer shows something of all of them, and the oldest saint is still growing in every one.

What does adding self-control actually look like? Start with one appetite that rules you: food, the phone, anger, spending, sleep, lust. Decide in advance, in the light of God’s word, what obedience looks like there; remove what feeds it; tell a trusted believer and ask him to ask you. When you fail, confess at once, receive forgiveness, and go again the same day. Self-control is not gritted teeth alone but the Spirit’s fruit (Galatians 5:23), growing as you rely on him in specific, repeated choices.

verseByVerse.quote: For if these qualities are yours and are increasing, they keep you from being ineffective or unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. For whoever lacks these qualities is so nearsighted that he is blind, having forgotten that he was cleansed from his former sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where these qualities are growing, a believer’s knowledge of Christ bears fruit; where they are missing, he has become short-sighted to the point of blindness, because he has forgotten that his sins were washed away.

Yours and increasing. Increasing, pleonazonta, means abounding. Peter assumes growth is normal, and a static Christian life already a warning sign. A tree that has not grown for years is either very old or dead.

Ineffective or unfruitful. Ineffective, argous, is literally idle, like the workers standing in the marketplace (Matthew 20:3); unfruitful, akarpous, is barren. These qualities do not earn knowledge, but without them a man’s knowing goes nowhere. You may hold the doctrine accurately and be entirely unproductive in it, like the best soil in the county that nobody has sown.

So nearsighted that he is blind. Myopic comes from this word (myōpazōn). The man sees perfectly well what is in front of him: this week, this appetite, this grievance, this pay rise. What he cannot see is anything at a distance: eternity, the judgment seat, the coming kingdom, the souls around him. Short-sightedness left alone becomes blindness, the false teachers’ disease exactly: they scoff at the Lord’s coming (3:4) because they cannot see past their own desires.

Having forgotten that he was cleansed. This is the root of the trouble. Forgotten is literally having taken forgetfulness (lēthēn labōn), as though he had picked it up and put it on. Cleansed, katharismos, is Christ’s purification for sins, made once, by himself, before he sat down (Hebrews 1:3). No stain is left half-washed, and no former sin is kept in reserve against his people. He has lost not necessarily the cleansing but the memory of it, and with it the fuel for growth, since gratitude drives the whole chain of verses 5–7. The woman who washed Jesus’ feet with her tears loved much because she knew she had been forgiven much (Luke 7:47). When growth has stopped, look for a memory gone dim, not a missing technique.

In everyday life. Before you sleep tonight, lift your eyes past the next week to the day you will see Christ. Then remember one specific sin you have been forgiven, and thank him for it by name. The memory will do more for your growth than a new resolution.

I feel stuck and fruitless. Am I a Christian at all? That it troubles you is a good sign; the man Peter describes is not troubled but drowsy. Begin where Peter puts the problem, with memory. Go back to the cross and see again what your sins cost and how freely they were washed away (read a Gospel slowly, or Psalm 103, or Isaiah 53). Confess the specific sins that have choked growth, then take one step of obedience in one quality of verses 5–7. Fruit grows slowly and is often seen first by others, so ask a mature believer what they see. And do not judge your whole standing by one dry season; judge it by where you run.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, brothers, be all the more diligent to confirm your calling and election, for if you practice these qualities you will never fall. For in this way there will be richly provided for you an entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So keep growing, and you will become ever surer that God has called and chosen you; those who live this way will never fall away, and will be welcomed lavishly into Christ’s eternal kingdom. Diligence does not make God’s choice firm; it makes us sure of it.

Be all the more diligent. Be diligent, spoudasate, echoes verse 5, and “all the more” raises it. “Brothers” appears only here in the letter: after the warning, a brother pleading with brothers.

To confirm your calling and election. Confirm, bebaian poieisthai, means to make firm; a related word was a legal term for ratifying a contract. Calling is God’s effectual call; election, eklogē, his eternal choice. Calling comes first because through it we learn of the choice made before time. We cannot make our election more certain to God; it is fixed. But we can make it more certain to ourselves, by growing in the qualities of verses 5–7, the evidence of genuine faith. The fruit does not create the root; it shows the root is there. Good works do not make us saved; they make us sure.

You will never fall. Practise, poiountes, is present tense: keep doing. Never fall, ou mē ptaisēte pote, is a strong double negative: you will certainly never stumble. It promises not sinlessness but that you will never come to ruin, never fall away and be lost. We still stumble daily in lesser ways; but Christ obeyed perfectly in our place, his righteousness is counted as ours (Romans 5:19), and our faltering practice is accepted for his sake.

Richly provided. The chorēgos word of verse 5 again (plousiōs epichorēgēthēsetai), now in reverse: they were to supply these qualities lavishly; God will lavishly supply their entrance. Entrance, eisodos, is a welcome, like a victorious general’s through the city gates: not scraping in “as through fire” (1 Corinthians 3:15) as the door shuts, but a son coming home to a feast, into the kingdom no false teacher can scoff away.

Of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. The same construction as verse 1: one person, Lord and Saviour, and the way in is his doing. He entered once for all into the holy places by his own blood, securing an eternal redemption (Hebrews 9:12), and went to prepare a place for his disciples, promising to come again and take them to himself (John 14:2–3). The entrance is rich because the King has gone through the gate ahead of his people, and he is the one standing at it.

He keeps those he calls. Before the world was made he chose us, and in time his voice found us and called us by name. He keeps those he calls, so that the one who stumbled on a dark night by a courtyard fire could write, half a lifetime later, “you will never fall.”

The kindness in it. An anxious Christian is not told to search his memory for a decisive moment or look inward for a feeling, but to look for growth in ordinary character, visible to others as well as to him. We are not left to guess at God’s secret choice; we look at what he is doing in us.

Does “if you practice these qualities” mean that perseverance depends on our effort? No. The qualities are the fruit of the divine power that has given us all we need (v. 3), and those who belong to Christ are kept by him; diligence is the way his keeping works out in our lives, not a rival to it.

Can a true Christian fall away and be lost? No. Those God has chosen and called he keeps, and none will be snatched out of Christ’s hand (John 10:28–29; Romans 8:30; Philippians 1:6). True believers can fall into serious sin for a time, as Peter did when he denied the Lord, losing the joy of salvation under the Father’s discipline; but they are brought back, because Christ prays for them as he prayed for Peter (Luke 22:32). Those who abandon the faith altogether show that they never truly belonged (1 John 2:19). Many faithful Christians in the Arminian and Wesleyan traditions hold that a believer can freely turn away and be lost, and rightly take Scripture’s warnings seriously; this commentary holds the Reformed view of perseverance because of promises like John 10:28–29, while honouring them as brothers. So this promise is not a reason to relax but a reason to keep going without fear.

What if I look and cannot see the fruit? First, look at Christ before you look at yourself: assurance rests first on his promise to receive all who come (John 6:37), not on your inspection. Second, look honestly but not morbidly; fruit is often small, slow and more visible to others. Do you trust him? Do you want to obey him? Do you grieve over sin? Do you love his people? Third, if you find almost nothing, do not sit down in despair: go to Christ now as a sinner, and begin to obey. Your calling is confirmed not by endless self-examination but by present faith and diligence.

Where Christians differ: can I know I am elect? Some fear election makes assurance impossible: how can I know if God chose me? Others think assurance comes only by special revelation. This commentary’s view: believers can and should have assurance of their election. It is grounded first in God’s promises in Christ, received by faith, and confirmed by the Spirit’s inner witness (Romans 8:16) and the fruit of a godly life (1 John 2:3; 3:14). Election is a cause not for anxiety but for confidence: those who trust Christ and grow in godliness may know they are chosen (1 Thessalonians 1:4–5). And the elect will persevere: they will never fall.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–21 — Eyewitnesses and the Prophetic Word
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The message Peter’s readers believed is true, and it rests on firmer ground than any teacher’s novelty. Facing the death Jesus foretold, Peter will keep reminding them of what they already know, and wants them to remember it when he is gone (vv. 12–15). Their faith rests on two witnesses that agree: the apostles, who saw Christ’s majesty and heard the Father’s voice on the holy mountain, a preview of his coming (vv. 16–18), and the prophetic word, a lamp in a dark place until Christ the morning star rises (v. 19), which came not from human will but from men carried along by the Holy Spirit (vv. 20–21).
verseByVerse.theology:
Carried Along

Prophecy did not come from the prophet’s own interpretation. Men spoke from God as the Holy Spirit carried them along: fully human, and fully God’s word.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter wrote knowing his death was near, and arranged for his readers to remember.

Now: Scripture is a lamp in a dark place, enough light until the day dawns.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I intend always to remind you of these qualities, though you know them and are established in the truth that you have. I think it right, as long as I am in this body, to stir you up by way of reminder, since I know that the putting off of my body will be soon, as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me. And I will make every effort so that after my departure you may be able at any time to recall these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing he will soon die, as Jesus told him, Peter will keep reminding his readers of truths they already know, and is making sure they can recall them after he is gone.

I intend always to remind you. Remind, hypomimnēskein, means keep reminding, a key theme of the letter (1:12, 13, 15; 3:1–2). They know these things, and he will keep saying them, against the appetite for novelty the false teachers exploited. Knowing a thing and having it present to you are different. A man knows he loves his wife; he still needs to remember it at six o’clock on a tiring evening.

Established in the truth. Established, estērigmenous, is perfect tense: settled and still standing. It is the word Jesus used to Peter on the night of the denial: “when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32). The man who could not stand firm for a night spends his last days making others firm.

As long as I am in this body. Body, skēnōma, is literally tent, struck when the journey moves on (2 Corinthians 5:1–4). Stir you up, diegeirein, means to wake someone, as the disciples woke Jesus in the storm (Luke 8:24; compare 3:1). His ministry is not filling empty heads but waking drowsy ones.

The putting off of my body. Laying aside, as one takes off clothing (apothesis). Death lays aside the body, not the person, and Peter speaks of it calmly.

As our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me. On the beach, after the third question about love, Jesus told Peter that when he was old others would stretch out his hands and lead him where he did not want to go, showing by what kind of death he would glorify God (John 21:18–19). The stretched-out hands meant crucifixion, and early tradition says Peter was crucified in Rome under Nero. He was told on the morning of his restoration, when Jesus said, “Follow me”, and he has followed ever since, toward that death, with open eyes.

After my departure. Departure, exodos, is Luke’s word for what Moses and Elijah discussed with Jesus on the mountain: the departure he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). Peter had heard them. Because Jesus accomplished his exodus, every believer’s exodus is safe: a tent folded, a door opened, a servant at home with his Master. And Peter is arranging for his readers to remember after he has gone, perhaps by this letter itself, or by Mark’s Gospel, which early tradition says records Peter’s preaching.

In everyday life. Who will remember Christ better because of you: your children, a younger believer, a friend? A few lines telling one of them what Christ has been to you may outlast much else you leave, and you need not be dying to write them.

Is it not boring to hear the same things again and again? Only if hearing is for collecting information. Nobody calls bread boring; we need it again because we used up the last meal. Yesterday’s assurance does not carry today’s temptation; a heart that leaks needs the truth brought fresh. A good preacher finds new ways to say old things, but be wary of a teacher whose selling point is something nobody has heard before. In Christian truth, what is new is seldom true, and what is true is never stale to a hungry soul.

How should a Christian think about his own death? As Peter did: a tent folded and an exodus, not the end. To be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8), at once, not in a sleep or a purgatory, but with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23). To fear the pain and the parting is no sin; even Jesus was in anguish in the garden. But death has lost its sting (1 Corinthians 15:55–57), so use the time well. Peter’s question was not “How long have I left?” but “What will they remember when I am gone?” Ask the same.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus had told Peter how he would die.

verseByVerse.quote: For we did not follow cleverly devised myths when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty. For when he received honor and glory from God the Father, and the voice was borne to him by the Majestic Glory, "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased," we ourselves heard this very voice borne from heaven, for we were with him on the holy mountain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The coming of Christ that Peter preached is no invented tale: he saw Christ’s majesty with his own eyes and heard the Father’s voice on the holy mountain.

Not cleverly devised myths. Cleverly devised, sesophismenois, means made up. The false teachers evidently called Christ’s coming a tale to frighten people into good behaviour. Peter replies with history: myths were set in a timeless past no one could check; the gospel names a governor, a city, a mountain, and men who were there.

The power and coming. Probably his powerful coming (dynamin kai parousian): the second coming the false teachers denied (3:4). Parousia was used of a king’s state visit, and the apostles had already seen a preview of it.

Eyewitnesses of his majesty. Eyewitnesses (epoptai) was a word of the mystery religions for those admitted to the highest grade of initiation: those who had seen. Peter takes it from the cults, with their secret rites and private visions, for something that happened on a mountain in daylight before three fishermen. Majesty, megaleiotēs, is Luke’s word for the majesty of God that astonished the crowds at Jesus’ healing (Luke 9:43).

Honor and glory from God the Father. Peter is describing the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:1–8; Mark 9:2–8; Luke 9:28–36), where he was one of three disciples present. The honour was the Father’s word about him; the glory was the Son’s own radiance shining out.

The Majestic Glory. A reverent name for God, perhaps the bright cloud of his presence that filled the tabernacle, come down again on the mountain. When the disciples heard the voice they fell on their faces, terrified (Matthew 17:6); holiness that near is not cosy. Then Jesus touched them and told them to rise and not be afraid (Matthew 17:7): the glory that flattens sinners belongs to the one who lifts them up.

My beloved Son. The words echo Psalm 2:7, Isaiah 42:1 and Jesus’ baptism (Matthew 3:17). Peter reports not the shining face or Moses and Elijah but the voice, because his argument concerns testimony. The Father himself named Jesus his Son, the King of Psalm 2 and the Servant of Isaiah 42, and declared his delight in him.

On the holy mountain. Made holy by God’s presence as Sinai once was (tradition says Tabor; Hermon fits the Gospels well). There is something moving in the restraint. Peter had wanted to build three shelters and stay, not knowing what he said (Luke 9:33). He mentions none of that. Decades on he reports only what a witness may testify: we were there, and we heard.

The King’s face. On the mountain the curtain was drawn back for a moment, and the carpenter of Nazareth stood in the glory that was his before the world existed: Peter saw the King’s face as it will be seen on the day he comes. Then the beloved Son, whose face shone like the sun, came down the mountain to go to a cross, and he will come again in the same majesty, hidden from no one.

In everyday life. When someone dismisses the faith as a nice story, do not be rattled or defensive. Say plainly that Christianity stands or falls on events witnessed by named men, and offer to read one of the Gospels with them.

Why does the Transfiguration prove that Christ will come again? Because it was the coming in miniature. Jesus had just said that some standing there would not taste death until they saw the Son of Man coming in his kingdom (Matthew 16:28), and six days later three of them saw the glory he will have when he comes. The scoffers said the King would never come in power; Peter has already seen the King in his power. What was uncovered for a moment on the mountain will be revealed to the whole world on the last day.

How do we know the apostles were not simply mistaken or lying? Consider what their testimony cost: men do not willingly die for what they know to be a lie, and Peter writes under the shadow of crucifixion. Nor were they merely sincere; they claimed to have seen and heard for themselves, so they were in a position to know. Even for scholars who think a follower wrote this letter, three Gospels report the Transfiguration, in sober accounts full of the apostles’ own failures, written within living memory, when others could contradict them. And the witnesses are many: three on the mountain, hundreds who saw the risen Christ (1 Corinthians 15:6). Faith is not a leap in the dark but trust in reliable witnesses, confirmed by the Spirit who opens our eyes to see that what they say is true.

Isn’t it a beautiful myth, whether or not it happened? Many people kindly call the Gospels myths, true the way a great novel is true, whatever did or did not occur. But a myth can inspire you; it cannot rescue you, because only something that happened can change what has happened to you. C. S. Lewis, a literary scholar by profession, put it bluntly in an essay on modern biblical criticism: “I have been reading poems, romances, vision-literature, legends, myths all my life. I know what they are like. I know that not one of them is like this.” Legends float free of time and place; the Gospels name towns and officials and record their tellers’ failures. Richard Bauckham has argued (Jesus and the Eyewitnesses, 2006) that they rest on named witnesses still alive to be asked. Lewis’s own conclusion, in an essay of 1944, was that here myth became fact: what the old stories only dreamed of happened once, in history, under Pontius Pilate. A story can move you. Only a Saviour who really lived and rose can come for you.

Should I seek experiences of glory like Peter’s? No. Peter, having had the greatest experience a man could have, points his readers not to experiences but to the prophetic word (v. 19). The Transfiguration was given to chosen witnesses to found the church’s testimony, and written down so that you may believe without seeing (John 20:29). God may give deep joy and a sense of his nearness, and we thank him for it, but our faith rests on what happened and what is written, not on what we feel.
verseByVerse.note: The “holy mountain” is the Mount of Transfiguration, where Peter, James and John saw Jesus’ glory.

verseByVerse.quote: And we have the prophetic word more fully confirmed, to which you will do well to pay attention as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Scriptures that foretold Christ are an utterly reliable word, and believers should keep their eyes on them like a lamp in a dark place until Christ comes like the morning star.

The prophetic word more fully confirmed. The prophetic word is the Old Testament Scriptures as a whole, which foretell Christ, including his coming in glory. More fully confirmed, bebaioteron, is from the same family as the word for confirming your calling (v. 10). However the phrase is taken (see “Uncertain wording” below), Peter is not belittling what he saw; but his readers, who were not on the mountain and never would be, are told that what they hold in their hands is the firmest ground there is.

You will do well to pay attention. Pay attention, prosechontes: hold the mind on it, as a sailor keeps his eyes on a harbour light.

A lamp shining in a dark place. Lamp, lychnos, is a small oil lamp; the dark place is this world, and Scripture is the lamp (Psalm 119:105). A lamp is not the sun; it shows the next few feet. Peter is honest about how much light Scripture gives in this age: sufficient, and not yet daylight. We do not see everything. We see enough to walk.

Until the day dawns. The day of Christ’s return (Romans 13:12): the lamp is temporary, and a morning is coming.

The morning star. The light-bearer (phōsphoros) is the planet Venus, the last light before sunrise and its herald. It points to Christ himself, the bright morning star (Revelation 22:16; compare Numbers 24:17), so the dawn is his coming, the very thing the false teachers denied. “In your hearts” is a surprise, since his coming will be public: when Christ appears he will also fill his people’s hearts with light, and they will know him fully (1 Corinthians 13:12). Until then, we need the lamp.

Shining toward one Person. God has not left us in the dark. He lit a lamp and put it in our hands, and every page of it shines toward one Person. One day the lamp will be set down, not because it failed, but because the Sun himself has come, and we shall see him whom we have loved without seeing.

How do I pay attention to the lamp? Peter means a steady holding of the mind, not a glance. Keep it near. A lamp in the cupboard gives no light: read some Scripture every day, even a few verses, at a time you can actually keep. Read slowly. Ask of one sentence what it shows you of God and of Christ, and what it asks of you. Read towards Christ. The prophets searched for the sufferings of Christ and the glories to follow (1 Peter 1:10–11); look for him, and the lamp will show you the road he walked. Carry a line into the dark. Take one verse into the hardest part of the day and say it over when the dark presses in. Do it in hope rather than as a chore: the morning star is coming, and every page you attend to now trains your eyes to know him when the day dawns.

Is Scripture really more certain than seeing something with my own eyes? Yes, in this sense: eyes can be deceived, memories fade, and experiences need interpreting, but God’s written word does not change and cannot lie. Peter’s experience was real, yet it lasted minutes, was seen by three men, and needed words from God to explain it; Scripture is God’s permanent testimony for every believer in every age. So when an experience, a dream, an impression or a strong feeling seems to say one thing and Scripture another, Scripture wins every time. That is not distrust of God’s work in us; it is trust in his clearest word to us.

Does God still speak today apart from the Bible? This commentary holds that the gifts of new revelation, prophecy in the sense of authoritative words from God, ceased with the apostles, and that the canon of Scripture is closed (Hebrews 1:1–2; Jude 3). The apostles and prophets were the church’s foundation, laid once (Ephesians 2:20). Many dear brothers in Christ believe otherwise, and we hold our view with charity. But Bible-believing Christians widely agree on the practical point: Scripture is the lamp, sufficient for faith and life, and nothing claiming to be from God may add to it or contradict it. The Spirit does speak today, through the word he inspired, applying it to our hearts. If you want to hear God speak, open the Bible.

Uncertain wording. “More fully confirmed” can mean that the Transfiguration has confirmed the prophecies, so that they stand firmer still, or that the prophetic word is itself more reliable than Peter’s experience. The Greek allows both. The ESV leans to the first; the second fits verses 20–21, where Scripture comes from God himself. Either way the written word is sure ground. The word for “dark”, auchmēros, occurs only here in the New Testament; it means dry and dirty, a squalid, gloomy place where nothing grows.

verseByVerse.quote: knowing this first of all, that no prophecy of Scripture comes from someone's own interpretation. For no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Above all, know that no prophecy in Scripture began as a prophet’s own idea: the prophets spoke from God, carried along by the Holy Spirit. So Scripture can be trusted as the false teachers, who speak from their own will, cannot.

Knowing this first of all. Of first importance: before anything else about Scripture, know where it came from.

Someone’s own interpretation. Interpretation, epilysis, means explanation, the solving of something obscure. Peter’s subject is where prophecy came from, for verse 21 begins with “For” and explains verse 20. Prophecy was not a gifted man’s insight into his times; the message came from God (see “Uncertain wording” below).

Never produced by the will of man. Produced, ēnechthē, means was carried. The negative is absolute: no prophet sat down and decided to write the word of God. Peter lays this down because of what comes next: as false prophets arose among the people, so false teachers will arise among his readers (2:1), men whose message does come from their own will and appetite. Ask of any teaching where it came from.

Men spoke from God. Two things held together. Men spoke: real people, with their own vocabulary, style and circumstances. Isaiah does not sound like Amos; Paul does not sound like John. And they spoke from God: the message originated with him.

Carried along by the Holy Spirit. A sailing word (pheromenoi), used in Acts 27:15 and 17 of Paul’s ship, driven before the wind when it could no longer steer, and the verb used of the voice “borne from heaven” (vv. 17–18). The men are not passive cargo; they work the vessel and raise the sails. But the Spirit supplied power and direction, and across fifteen centuries, through shepherds and kings, prophets and fishermen, in palaces and in exile, they arrived where the wind took them. This is inspiration: Scripture is God-breathed (2 Timothy 3:16), fully human and fully divine in authorship, so that what it says, God says. And because God cannot lie (Numbers 23:19), Scripture is inerrant: whatever it affirms is true, in its history as much as in its doctrine.

The Spirit of Christ in them. Peter had written that the Spirit of Christ in the prophets was indicating the sufferings of Christ and the subsequent glories (1 Peter 1:11). The wind that drove the prophetic ship blew from Christ and toward Christ. Peter learned that reading from Christ himself, who on the Emmaus road, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27), and who said that Scripture cannot be broken (John 10:35). The Christian receives the Bible as the Lord Jesus received it: every word from God, and every page about him.

In everyday life. Before you open Scripture today, ask the Spirit who carried its writers to open your eyes. And when the word rebukes you, do not argue with the wind; set your sails by it.

Does this mean that individual Christians may not interpret Scripture for themselves? Roman Catholic teaching has used the verse to argue that the church alone can interpret Scripture rightly, but Peter is speaking of where prophecy came from, not how readers later handle it. Every believer is to read and understand Scripture (Acts 17:11), humbly, in the fellowship of the church and with its teachers, testing all interpretation by Scripture itself.

Does this apply to the New Testament too? Yes. Peter speaks here of Old Testament prophecy, but he sets the commandment of the apostles beside the prophets (3:2) and Paul’s letters among the other Scriptures (3:15–16). The Spirit who carried the prophets was promised to the apostles, to bring Jesus’ words to their remembrance and guide them into all the truth (John 14:26; 16:13). The church did not make these books Scripture; it recognised its Shepherd’s voice in them. With the apostles’ writings the canon is complete (see the note on v. 19).

What about the parts of the Bible that seem to contradict each other or science? Take them seriously and humbly. Many apparent contradictions dissolve under careful reading: writers choosing different details, round numbers, ancient ways of summarising speeches, or ordinary language for what the eye sees, as we still say the sun rises. Some difficulties remain unsolved, as good scholars honestly say; but a difficulty is not an error, and many supposed errors of a century ago have since been answered. When you meet one, keep reading, ask a mature teacher, consult a good commentary, and trust the God who cannot lie (Titus 1:2).

Where Christians differ: is Scripture fully inspired and without error? Some hold that Scripture is inspired only in its religious teaching, or that it contains human errors alongside divine truth. This commentary’s view: because Scripture came from God through men carried along by the Spirit, it shares God’s truthfulness. It is inerrant in all that it affirms, infallible in its teaching, and sufficient for faith and life. The human authors were not mere typewriters; God used their personalities and research (Luke 1:1–4). But the Spirit so guided them that what they wrote is the very word of God (1 Thessalonians 2:13). Sola Scriptura: Scripture is the final authority over every tradition, experience and claim of revelation.

Uncertain wording. Whose “own interpretation”: the prophet’s or the reader’s? Epilysis occurs only here in the New Testament (the related verb is used of Jesus explaining his parables, Mark 4:34). Many take it of the reader, as if no one may interpret prophecy on his own. But verse 21 explains verse 20 by describing how prophecy arose, not how it is read, so the likelier meaning is that no prophet produced his message from his own understanding of events.

Textual note. The KJV’s “holy men of God spake” follows later manuscripts; the earliest read “men spoke from God”, as most modern Bibles do.

1.theology:
The chapter’s great claim is that believers become partakers of the divine nature (v. 4): moral sharing, not deification (see the note on vv. 3–4). Calvin read it as a sharing in God’s qualities, not in his essence.

The doctrine of Scripture is equally central (see the notes on vv. 19 and 20–21).
1.examples:
The chain of virtues (vv. 5–7) speaks to Christians who stop at faith and see no need to grow. Peter’s answer: faith is the beginning, not the destination. The virtues are not the condition of salvation (they flow from faith, not to it) but the evidence that it is real and the direction of its growth.

The lamp (v. 19) helps believers who find Bible reading dry. You read it not because it is always exciting but because you are in a dark place and it is the lamp God has given.

keyVerse.quote: His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us to his own glory and excellence
keyVerse.note: Everything else in the chapter stands on this verse. The call to “make every effort” (v. 5) rests on what God has already given, so the Christian life is growth into a gift, not a climb toward one. And because God has already provided everything, no teacher can offer a missing piece; what we need is to know Christ better.

1.reflection:
Peter tells ordinary believers that their faith is “of equal standing” with an apostle’s (v. 1). Why is that true, and who in your church most needs to hear it?

Verse 3 says God has already given us everything for life and godliness, and verse 5 says “make every effort”. How do the two fit together? Where does your own effort tend to slide into either anxious earning or careless drift?

Peter traces a stalled Christian life to forgetting that we were cleansed (v. 9). How does remembering what you have been forgiven change the way you grow? What helps you remember?

Peter rests our faith on eyewitnesses and on Scripture, “a lamp shining in a dark place” (vv. 16–21). How would you answer a friend who says the Gospels are beautiful myths? What would it look like to pay closer attention to the lamp this week?

2.title: The Anatomy of a False Teacher
2.text: <sup>1</sup>But false prophets also arose among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you, who will secretly bring in destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them, bringing upon themselves swift destruction.<sup>2</sup>And many will follow their sensuality, and because of them the way of truth will be blasphemed.<sup>3</sup>And in their greed they will exploit you with false words. Their condemnation from long ago is not idle, and their destruction is not asleep.<sup>4</sup>For if God did not spare angels when they sinned, but cast them into hell and committed them to chains of gloomy darkness to be kept until the judgment;<sup>5</sup>if he did not spare the ancient world, but preserved Noah, a herald of righteousness, with seven others, when he brought a flood upon the world of the ungodly;<sup>6</sup>if by turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes he condemned them to extinction, making them an example of what is going to happen to the ungodly;<sup>7</sup>and if he rescued righteous Lot, greatly distressed by the sensual conduct of the wicked<sup>8</sup>(for as that righteous man lived among them day after day, he was tormenting his righteous soul over their lawless deeds that he saw and heard);<sup>9</sup>then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials, and to keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment,<sup>10</sup>and especially those who indulge in the lust of defiling passion and despise authority. Bold and willful, they do not tremble as they blaspheme the glorious ones,<sup>11</sup>whereas angels, though greater in might and power, do not pronounce a blasphemous judgment against them before the Lord.<sup>12</sup>But these, like irrational animals, creatures of instinct, born to be caught and destroyed, blaspheming about matters of which they are ignorant, will also be destroyed in their destruction,<sup>13</sup>suffering wrong as the wage for their wrongdoing. They count it pleasure to revel in the daytime. They are blots and blemishes, reveling in their deceptions, while they feast with you.<sup>14</sup>They have eyes full of adultery, insatiable for sin. They entice unsteady souls. They have hearts trained in greed. Accursed children!<sup>15</sup>Forsaking the right way, they have gone astray. They have followed the way of Balaam, the son of Beor, who loved gain from wrongdoing,<sup>16</sup>but was rebuked for his own transgression; a speechless donkey spoke with human voice and restrained the prophet's madness.<sup>17</sup>These are waterless springs and mists driven by a storm. For them the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved.<sup>18</sup>For, speaking loud boasts of folly, they entice by sensual passions of the flesh those who are barely escaping from those who live in error.<sup>19</sup>They promise them freedom, but they themselves are slaves of corruption. For whatever overcomes a person, to that he is enslaved.<sup>20</sup>For if, after they have escaped the defilements of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, the last state has become worse for them than the first.<sup>21</sup>For it would have been better for them never to have known the way of righteousness than after knowing it to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them.<sup>22</sup>What the true proverb says has happened to them: "The dog returns to its own vomit, and the sow, after washing herself, returns to wallow in the mire."
2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 ended with the true prophets, men “carried along by the Holy Spirit” (1:21). Chapter 2 turns to their counterfeits, and chapter 3 will answer the scoffing these men spread about Christ’s return.

The message. False teachers will rise inside the church, and they are as doomed as they are dangerous; but the God who judges them knows how to rescue his own. They deny the Master who bought them, they trade on the flock for money and pleasure, and they sell a freedom that is really slavery. History proves that God neither overlooks such evil nor forgets the godly who grieve over it.

Why it was said. The danger had moved inside: teachers sitting at the church’s own feasts, promising freedom from moral restraint and laughing at the coming judgment (see the introduction). New converts were being lured back into the life they had left, and steadier believers may well have wondered why God allowed it and whether he would ever act.

How the chapter makes its case. Verses 1–3 name the teachers: their method (slipping error in alongside the truth), their doctrine (denying the Master), their appeal (sensuality) and their motive (greed); and their judgment is not asleep. Verses 4–10a give the proof in one long sentence: the angels who sinned, the ancient world and Sodom were judged, while Noah and Lot were rescued, so “the Lord knows how” to do both. Verses 10b–16 draw the teachers’ portrait: reckless toward the unseen world, ruled by appetite, trained in greed, walking Balaam’s road. Verses 17–22 expose their promise: waterless springs offering freedom while themselves enslaved, and ending, like the washed sow, back in the mud they never stopped loving. The key irony is verse 19, and the test of a teacher throughout is not how clever his words are but how he lives.

Where it leads. The chapter is lit from behind by “the Master who bought them” (v. 1). The judgments that fell on angels, a world and two cities were previews of the judgment that fell on Christ, and every rescue pictures what he purchased. The verdict “righteous”, spoken over a compromised man like Lot, can only be explained by the Righteous One whose record is counted for the unrighteous. And where false teachers wash the outside and leave the nature unchanged, Christ gives a new heart, so that his sheep return to their Shepherd and not to the mire.

For us. Test the teachers you listen to by what they do with Christ, how they live and what they want from you. If you are worn down by the evil around you, take Lot’s comfort: the Lord knows how to rescue you. And let the chapter’s last picture search you, not to make you anxious but honest: what do you keep returning to?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Arrival and Judgment of False Teachers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will not let false teachers go unpunished, and he will not let the godly be lost among them. Verses 1–3 warn that as Israel had false prophets, the church will have false teachers: inside the fellowship, denying the Master who bought them, popular because they excuse sin, and greedy. Verses 4–10a prove from history that their judgment is not asleep: God judged the angels who sinned, the ancient world and Sodom, yet rescued Noah and Lot. So the Lord knows how to rescue the godly and to hold the wicked for judgment, especially those who follow their appetites and despise his authority.
verseByVerse.theology:
Righteous Lot

False teachers arise from within. God did not spare the angels, the ancient world or Sodom, yet he preserved Noah and rescued Lot. He knows how to rescue the godly and to hold the unrighteous for judgment.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Lot, compromised as he was, was tormented by the evil he saw day after day.

Now: Being grieved by the world’s evil is a mark of the righteous; being comfortable with it is the danger.

verseByVerse.quote: But false prophets also arose among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you, who will secretly bring in destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them, bringing upon themselves swift destruction. And many will follow their sensuality, and because of them the way of truth will be blasphemed. And in their greed they will exploit you with false words. Their condemnation from long ago is not idle, and their destruction is not asleep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church will have false teachers, as Israel had false prophets, and their greed and denial of Christ are carrying them to a judgment already on its way.

The setting. Much of this chapter closely parallels the letter of Jude (see the introduction). The false teachers seem to have joined a denial of Christ’s return and judgment (3:3–4) to moral licence: since no judgment is coming, live as you please. They may have twisted Paul’s teaching on grace into permission to sin (3:15–16).

False prophets also arose. Many in Israel claimed to speak for God but did not (Deuteronomy 13:1–5; 18:20–22; Jeremiah 23:9–40). Every true prophet had his shadow: Moses had Balaam; Jeremiah had Hananiah and a crowd crying peace, peace, when there was no peace (Jeremiah 6:14). Israel had them; the church will have them.

False teachers among you. Inside the church, not outside (Acts 20:29–30; Matthew 7:15), which makes them dangerous and hard to name. A persecutor is easy to recognise; a false teacher sits in the next pew, sings the same hymns and uses the same vocabulary.

Secretly bring in destructive heresies. To smuggle in alongside (pareisaxousin). Error rarely arrives as a replacement for the truth, but as an addition placed beside it, until one day the truth has been edged out of the room. Heresies (haireseis) originally meant choices: a man’s own preference set up against what was delivered.

Denying the Master who bought them. Denying (arnoumenoi) is disowning, by teaching and by life (Titus 1:16; Jude 4). The word is painful on Peter’s lips: it is the word used of his own three denials in the courtyard. He knows what it is to deny the Lord and be brought back; these men deny him and have no tears. Master (despotēs) is the owner of slaves, and bought (agorasanta) is the market word for buying them (1 Corinthians 6:20): purchased slaves repudiating the man who paid for them, and bringing swift destruction on themselves.

Many will follow their sensuality. Sensuality (aselgeia) is shameless excess. False teaching is popular because it offers what our sinful nature already wants, and a sinful life looks for teaching that will excuse it. A teacher who promises comfort, success or freedom from rebuke is selling to an appetite already in the room (2 Timothy 4:3).

The way of truth will be blasphemed. The way of truth is the Christian faith (Acts 9:2). Outsiders judge it by the people carrying its name (Romans 2:24), and these readers were already being slandered (1 Peter 2:12).

In their greed they will exploit you. Greed (pleonexia) is the craving for more. Exploit (emporeusontai) is a trading word, from which comes emporium: they will make merchandise of you, and the congregation is the commodity. False words (plastois logois) are moulded words, from which comes plastic: shaped to sell rather than to tell the truth.

Not idle, not asleep. From long ago God has pronounced judgment on such people (Jude 4). Not idle (ouk argei) shares a root with “ineffective” in 1:8; not asleep (ou nystazei) is the word for the virgins who all grew drowsy (Matthew 25:5). Judgment has been on its way a long time, awake and moving. And God’s care for his sheep is awake too: he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep (Psalm 121:4).

What it does not mean. Not every theological disagreement is a destructive heresy. Peter means the denial of Christ, joined to immoral living and greed.

In everyday life. Test the teachers you listen to online and the books on your nightstand: does this make Christ greater to me, and me holier and more generous, or does it make me more comfortable with myself?

Were these men ever saved? The chapter suggests not: they enjoyed all the church gave, the preaching, the fellowship, the table, an outward cleaning-up, and went back to their old ways like a dog to its vomit (v. 22), because their nature had never changed. The lesson is not to puzzle over their secret state but to examine our own: do I merely belong to a church that Christ bought, or do I belong to Christ?

How can I tell a false teacher from a true one who makes mistakes? Peter names three tests. What does he do with Christ: deny his deity, lordship, atoning death or return, or exalt him? What does his teaching produce, in him and his followers: holiness or licence? Is he serving the flock or using it, for money, power or admiration? A sincere teacher may be wrong on secondary matters and still love Christ, live humbly and feed the sheep; treat him as a brother. One who denies Christ, excuses sin and enriches himself is what this chapter describes, however gifted.

What should I do if I suspect false teaching in my church? Do not gossip and do not panic. Test what is taught by Scripture, carefully and fairly (Acts 17:11; 1 John 4:1). If still concerned, speak privately to the person or to your elders, who are charged with guarding the flock (Acts 20:28–31; Titus 1:9), and be specific about what was said and why it troubles you. If the elders themselves teach what denies the gospel and will not be corrected, you may need to leave for a faithful church, quietly and without bitterness. Pray for those being misled, and keep your own heart close to Christ.

Where Christians differ: does “the Master who bought them” prove Christ died for everyone, including those who perish? Arminians (who hold that Christ died to make salvation possible for everyone, each person’s free response deciding the outcome) and some others, including some Calvinists, cite this verse to argue that Christ paid for the sins of all, even of those finally lost. The Reformed view, often called definite or particular atonement, is that Christ died to secure the salvation of his people. Godly believers have long differed here, and the debate is about how wide Christ’s purpose was, not whether his death is freely offered to all. This commentary’s view: The word is Master (despotēs), not Saviour or Redeemer: a slave-owner whose rightful ownership the teachers deny. Peter may be describing them by their own profession, as men who claimed to be bought by Christ; or he may be echoing Deuteronomy 32:6, where Israel as a nation is said to have been bought by God, though many Israelites were not saved. The verse does not use the language of effective redemption from sin (as 1 Peter 1:18–19 does). Scripture elsewhere teaches that Christ laid down his life for his sheep (John 10:11, 15), that his death actually secures the salvation of those for whom he died (Romans 8:32–34; Hebrews 10:14), and that the sheep are never lost (John 10:28). The best reading is that they professed to belong to the Master who purchased the church, and their denial exposed that profession as false.
verseByVerse.note: Much of this chapter closely parallels the letter of Jude.
