verseByVerse.quote: For if God did not spare angels when they sinned, but cast them into hell and committed them to chains of gloomy darkness to be kept until the judgment; if he did not spare the ancient world, but preserved Noah, a herald of righteousness, with seven others, when he brought a flood upon the world of the ungodly; if by turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes he condemned them to extinction, making them an example of what is going to happen to the ungodly;
verseByVerse.commentary:
History proves that rank, numbers and notoriety protect no one from God’s judgment. Yet even in the flood God kept those who were his.

If God did not spare angels. One long “if … then” sentence (vv. 4–9): three judgments, and woven among them two rescues. The first case is the highest of creatures: if rank protected anybody, it would have protected them.

Cast them into hell. Hell here is Tartarus (tartarōsas), found only here in the New Testament: the Greek name, familiar to his readers, for the deepest place of confinement.

Chains of gloomy darkness. Gloomy darkness (zophos) is the darkness of the underworld. Kept (tēroumenous): held in custody for a trial not yet held (Jude 6; Revelation 20:10). Not all demons are bound, since many are active (Ephesians 6:12); these particular angels are.

But preserved Noah. The ancient world is the world of the flood (Genesis 6–8), judged except for one family. A herald of righteousness (dikaiosynēs kēryx) is a preacher of righteousness. Genesis records no sermon, but Jewish tradition held that Noah warned his generation, and the ark itself was a proclamation: years of hammering in sight of neighbours who thought him mad. Eight survived (1 Peter 3:20). Faithfulness is not measured by numbers.

The world of the ungodly. Ungodly (asebōn): without regard for God. They were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day Noah entered the ark (Matthew 24:38).

Sodom and Gomorrah. Their sins included sexual immorality and violence (Genesis 19:4–9; Jude 7), and also pride, excess and neglect of the poor (Ezekiel 16:49–50). The three cases build: the highest creatures, the whole world, the most notorious cities.

An example. A pattern set out as a warning (hypodeigma), as the desolate country by the Dead Sea was in Jewish memory. Past judgments preview the final one (Luke 17:26–30).

Did not spare. The verb (ouk epheisato) is the one Paul uses of God not sparing his own Son (Romans 8:32). God did not spare the angels who sinned, because they deserved judgment; he did not spare his Son, who deserved none, so that he might spare us. Every judgment here points to the one that fell on Christ at Calvary, and every rescue pictures what his death purchased.

The LORD shut him in. The LORD shut Noah in with his own hand (Genesis 7:16), and then the rain came. Outside the ark the waters were judgment; inside, the same waters lifted eight people above a drowned world and set them down on a washed earth. Jesus called his death a baptism he had to undergo (Luke 12:50): the flood of judgment went over him, and those in him are carried through it into a new creation (1 Peter 3:21). He has never lost one soul that he shut in.

Is it not harsh to talk about judgment like this? Only if it were untrue, or said without tears. Judgment is not a flaw in God’s love but the expression of his holiness and justice; a God who never judged evil would not be good. And in Peter’s telling judgment comes with rescue, and after long patience: God waited while Noah built, and would have spared Sodom for ten righteous people (Genesis 18:32). Speaking of judgment is a kindness when it moves people to flee to Christ, who bore it in their place. The cruel thing would be silence.

Which angels are these? Some take them as the angels who fell with Satan at the beginning. Others, following Jewish tradition, link them with the sons of God who sinned with human women before the flood (Genesis 6:1–4), as Jude 6–7 may also do; and the order here (angels, flood, Sodom) follows Genesis, which suggests the Genesis 6 sin. Calvin and many Reformed writers read those sons of God as the godly line of Seth, and some as kings. Peter does not settle it, and neither does this commentary; faithful readers have held each view. Either way the point stands: if God did not spare angels, he will not spare false teachers.

Textual note. For chains (seirais) some manuscripts read sirois, pits.
verseByVerse.note: “Hell” here is Tartarus, a Greek term for the deepest place of punishment.

verseByVerse.quote: and if he rescued righteous Lot, greatly distressed by the sensual conduct of the wicked (for as that righteous man lived among them day after day, he was tormenting his righteous soul over their lawless deeds that he saw and heard); then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials, and to keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord knows how to rescue his people out of a wicked world, even a compromised believer like Lot, and how to hold the wicked for judgment. Here the sentence begun in verse 4 lands.

Righteous Lot. The surprise of the paragraph, for Genesis does not flatter Lot. He chose the well-watered plain and moved his tent as far as Sodom (Genesis 13:10–13); he offered his daughters to the mob (19:8); he lingered when told to flee, and had to be dragged out by the hand (19:16); and his family’s later story is squalid (19:30–38). Yet Peter calls him righteous three times in two verses. Lot was righteous by faith, as Abraham was (Genesis 19:15–16, 29). The word describes how he stood before God, not his record: if Lot is called righteous, it cannot mean an impressive life. Rescued (errysato) is the verb of the Lord’s Prayer: “deliver us from evil.”

Tormenting his righteous soul. Greatly distressed (kataponoumenon) is worn down. Peter’s evidence for Lot’s righteousness is entirely inward: Lot did little that was right, but the evil around him made him suffer. Genesis does not tell of this distress, though Lot did protest the men’s demands (19:7); Peter reveals it. Tormenting (ebasanizen) is the word for testing metal on a touchstone and for torment under interrogation, and “day after day” shows its kind: not one crisis but a daily wearing down, a man who had chosen to live there and could not stop being grieved by it. Believers today should likewise be grieved, not entertained, by the wickedness around them.

The Lord knows how to rescue. Knows how (oiden): the readers need not work out how he will do it. He provided an ark for Noah and a road out of the city for Lot. He hears the grief his people never speak aloud, and he will bring every one of them out, by the hand if he must, before the fire falls.

To keep the unrighteous under punishment. Keep (tērein) is the custody word of verse 4: the Lord who knows how to rescue also knows how to hold. The wicked dead are held for the final judgment (Luke 16:23–24), not being purified (see “Uncertain wording” below).

Rescued from the present evil age. Lot’s rescue pictures a greater one. Angels went into Sodom to bring one man out; the Son of God came into this world itself, and did not merely take us by the hand but gave himself for our sins to deliver us from the present evil age (Galatians 1:4). And the verdict righteous, spoken over a man with Lot’s record, has one explanation: God justifies the ungodly for the sake of the righteous one who suffered for the unrighteous (Romans 4:5; 1 Peter 3:18), counting Christ’s record as theirs. The Lord knows how to rescue, and at the cross he showed how.

A comfort for the compromised. If the mark of a righteous man in Sodom is that the place still distresses him, then a believer worn down by the evil around him, even one living with the results of poor choices, has in that distress a sign that he is God’s, not a reason to feel condemned. The comfortable are the ones in danger. And God rescued Lot though he lingered, “the LORD being merciful to him” (Genesis 19:16).

What it does not mean. Not that believers will always be spared suffering in this life, but that God will finally rescue them, through death if need be, and never abandon them.

What if I live, like Lot, somewhere I chose badly? Take comfort: God did not abandon Lot, and will not abandon you. Take warning too: Lot lost his possessions, his sons-in-law, his wife, and his daughters’ sense of right and wrong. Ask honestly whether your work, neighbourhood, friendships or entertainment are wearing down your love for God, or only wearing you down with grief. If the first, seek a way out; God may be providing one. If the second, stay faithful, and let your grief become prayer for the people around you.

How can I be grieved by the world without becoming bitter or self-righteous? Lot’s grief came from love of righteousness, not contempt for people. Grieve as one forgiven much, not as one who is better; pray for those whose deeds trouble you; and take your distress to God, not into endless complaint about the culture. A heart grieved by sin and full of mercy for sinners looks like Christ, who wept over Jerusalem.

Uncertain wording. Under punishment (kolazomenous) is a present participle, literally “being punished”. Some translations take it as looking ahead, “to be punished” at the judgment. But the present tense most naturally means punishment already under way, and that is the likelier reading: the wicked dead are conscious and held in custody, already suffering, until the day of judgment (compare Luke 16:23–24).
verseByVerse.note: Genesis does not tell of Lot’s inner distress, though Lot did call the men’s intent wicked (Gen 19:7); Peter draws out the inner side of it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–22 — The Portrait, and the Washed Sow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: See what these teachers are, and you will not want what they offer. Peter paints them without flattery: reckless toward unseen powers that even angels treat with care (vv. 10b–11), living by instinct and appetite at the church’s own feasts (vv. 12–14), greedy like Balaam (vv. 15–16), and promising freedom while enslaved to corruption (vv. 17–19). Having known the way of righteousness and turned back, they are worse off than before, like a washed sow back in the mud: cleaned, but never changed (vv. 20–22).
verseByVerse.theology:
Washed, Not Changed

The false teachers promise freedom while slaves of corruption. The washed sow returns to the mire because her nature was never changed.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Like Balaam, they loved gain and preyed on unsteady new believers.

Now: The question is not whether you have been washed, but whether you have been changed.

verseByVerse.quote: and especially those who indulge in the lust of defiling passion and despise authority. Bold and willful, they do not tremble as they blaspheme the glorious ones, whereas angels, though greater in might and power, do not pronounce a blasphemous judgment against them before the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The false teachers follow their appetites and despise the Lord’s authority, and they mock unseen powers that even mighty angels leave to God’s judgment.

Defiling passion. Indulge (poreuomenous) is literally walk after: their desires lead and they follow. Defiling passion is polluting lust. The first mark is appetite.

And despise authority. Authority (kyriotēs) is lordship. These men will be told nothing by anybody, and the two marks belong together: a man who wants to follow his appetites must first get rid of anyone with the right to say no.

Bold and willful. Bold (tolmētai) is reckless; willful (authadeis) is self-pleasing (Titus 1:7): a confidence with no outside check, which is exactly what makes a false teacher persuasive. Uncertain people are drawn to certainty, and these men never doubt themselves.

The glorious ones, whereas angels. Glories (doxas) are angelic beings, probably fallen angels, of whom the teachers speak with contempt, as men who have never considered that the unseen world might be real. Even holy angels, far stronger and knowing what these powers are, leave judgment to God: in a story known from Jewish tradition, the archangel Michael, disputing with the devil over Moses’ body, said, “The Lord rebuke you” (Jude 9). The teachers’ boldness is not courage but ignorance.

The lordship they despise. It is most naturally the Lord’s own: they deny the Master who bought them (v. 1), and Jude says the same men reject authority (Jude 8). Before that lordship an unclean spirit cried out in the synagogue at Capernaum, I know who you are, the Holy One of God, and was silenced with a word (Mark 1:24–25). Michael would not pronounce judgment on the devil because judgment belongs to the Lord, and the Father has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22). The men who joke about the powers are joking in front of their Judge, before whom the mightiest angels cover their faces.

How should a Christian deal with the devil, then? Firmly, humbly, and in Christ’s name, not our own. Resist him, firm in your faith (1 Peter 5:8–9; James 4:7). Put on the armour of God (Ephesians 6:10–18). Pray; flee temptation. You need not shout at demons, mock them or seek them out; Michael simply appealed to the Lord. Nor need you fear them: greater is he who is in you (1 John 4:4). The posture is quiet confidence in Christ’s victory, not bravado and not terror.

What about authority I genuinely disagree with? Despising authority is not disagreeing with it. You may question a decision, appeal respectfully, or, where an authority commands sin, obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). Where authority is abused, especially against the vulnerable, it must be exposed and the victims protected; that is not rebellion but righteousness. Peter condemns the settled heart that refuses to be under anyone, God included, so that it can do as it pleases.

Uncertain wording. Who “the glorious ones” are is not certain: most take them as fallen angels, some as holy angels, a few as human rulers. Verse 11 is compressed too: “against them” most likely means against these evil powers, as Michael would not slander the devil (Jude 9), though some take “them” as the false teachers. The reading followed above is the likeliest.

verseByVerse.quote: But these, like irrational animals, creatures of instinct, born to be caught and destroyed, blaspheming about matters of which they are ignorant, will also be destroyed in their destruction, suffering wrong as the wage for their wrongdoing. They count it pleasure to revel in the daytime. They are blots and blemishes, reveling in their deceptions, while they feast with you. They have eyes full of adultery, insatiable for sin. They entice unsteady souls. They have hearts trained in greed. Accursed children!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Living by appetite like animals, the false teachers will be destroyed by the corruption they practise, even while they sit at the church’s fellowship meals.

Like irrational animals. Irrational (aloga) is logos, reason, with “not” in front. They have exchanged reason for instinct, which is why arguing with them achieves nothing. Believers were made partakers of the divine nature (1:4); these men have sunk to living by instinct.

Born to be caught and destroyed. Like wild animals that end in the hunter’s trap, men who live by appetite follow their nose to the bait and never see the snare. They speak loudest about what they understand least, and the ruin they bring on others is the ruin they receive.

Suffering wrong as the wage. A wordplay: they are paid with harm for the harm they did. They wanted wages, and they will get them (compare Balaam, v. 15).

To revel in the daytime. Revel (tryphē) is luxurious indulgence. Even in a Greek city serious drinking belonged to the night (1 Thessalonians 5:7); these men indulge in broad daylight. Shame has gone.

Eyes full of adultery. Literally eyes full of an adulteress: men who cannot look at a woman without sizing her up as a conquest (Matthew 5:28). Insatiable (akatapaustous) is never resting, the cruelty of every lust: it promises rest and delivers restlessness.

They entice unsteady souls. Entice (deleazontes) is to bait (James 1:14). Unsteady (astēriktous) is the opposite of the established believers of 1:12.

Hearts trained in greed. Trained (gegymnasmenēn) is the athlete’s word, the root of gymnasium: not a lapse but a practised habit. The same word describes mature believers’ trained discernment (Hebrews 5:14). Everyone is in training for something.

Accursed children! Literally children of a curse. Not a loss of temper but a cry of horror at what these men have become, and where they are taking others.

Blots and blemishes, while they feast with you. They are stains on the church’s fellowship meals, turning them into self-indulgence. Yet believers were ransomed with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Peter 1:19), and Peter will urge them to be found without spot or blemish (3:14). The spotless Lamb died to have a spotless people (Ephesians 5:25–27), and here are blemished men at the very meals where the church remembered him.

Exactly the people he came for. Every line of this portrait has its opposite in him. His eyes were full of compassion, never of lust; he did not bait the unsteady but gathered them, and carried the lambs in his arms. And children of a curse are exactly the people he came for. He bore the curse himself, so that the accursed might be called children of God and sit at his table, washed, filled and welcome.

In everyday life. Ask what your habits are training you in: what you watch, scroll, spend on and daydream about. Not by willpower alone: the Spirit trains you through the word, prayer and the company of believers, so replace one sinful habit with one habit of grace. You will not do it perfectly. Christ’s clean eyes and pure heart were his obedience in your place, counted as yours; so when you fail, begin again.

Why is the Bible’s language about these men so harsh? Because they are leading souls to destruction while feasting at the Lord’s Table, and a shepherd who finds wolves among the flock does not describe them gently (Acts 20:29; compare Matthew 23). The harshness is love for the sheep. But it is aimed at those who teach and exploit; to the weak and wandering Scripture speaks with great tenderness (Matthew 12:20).

I struggle with lustful eyes. Am I like these men? A believer who fights lust and hates it is a world away from a man whose eyes are full of it, who is insatiable, trains himself in it and teaches others to indulge. The first is a wounded soldier; the second a deserter. A believer can love a sin and hate it at once, and that inner war is itself the Spirit’s work (Romans 7:15–25; Galatians 5:17). Keep fighting: make a covenant with your eyes (Job 31:1), cut off what feeds it, bring it into the light with a trusted believer, and run to Christ each time you fall. Your grief shows you are not what this verse describes.

Uncertain wording. In their destruction (en tē phthora autōn) can be read two ways. “Their” may be the animals: the teachers will be destroyed as beasts are. Or it may be the teachers: they will be destroyed in their own corruption, the word used in 1:4 and 2:19. Both make sense and come to the same end, and the play on words is deliberate either way.

Textual note. For deceptions (apatais) some manuscripts read agapais, love feasts, as in Jude 12.

verseByVerse.quote: Forsaking the right way, they have gone astray. They have followed the way of Balaam, the son of Beor, who loved gain from wrongdoing, but was rebuked for his own transgression; a speechless donkey spoke with human voice and restrained the prophet's madness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like Balaam, the false teachers know God’s way and have left it for money, a madness even a donkey could see.

Forsaking the right way. Gone astray (eplanēthēsan) gives us planet, a wandering star. They knew the road, and they left it.

The way of Balaam. Balaam fits these teachers exactly: a soothsayer to whom God really spoke (Joshua 13:22; Numbers 22:9–12), who put that gift on the market. Balak of Moab offers money to have Israel cursed; Balaam wants the fee, but every time he opens his mouth, blessing comes out (Numbers 22–24). God would not let him curse, because the LORD loved his people (Deuteronomy 23:5), and no hired prophet or enemy can curse those whom he has blessed. Balaam later advised Balak how to lead Israel into sexual immorality and idolatry at Peor (Numbers 25:1–3; 31:16; Revelation 2:14), and that is what he is remembered for (Jude 11).

Who loved gain from wrongdoing. Literally loved the wages of unrighteousness, echoing verse 13: not men who set out to destroy the church but men who discovered that religion pays and adjusted their message to keep it paying. The problem was not that Balaam was paid, but what he loved.

A speechless donkey. The prophet behaves like an animal, so an animal does the prophet’s job (Numbers 22:21–35). Madness (paraphronia) is being out of one’s mind. Balaam was not deceived; he had heard from God repeatedly and went anyway. The man who knows what God has said and calculates that the money is worth it has lost his reason, whatever his gifts.

A star out of Jacob. The most remarkable thing Balaam ever said, he said against his will: “I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near: a star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel” (Numbers 24:17). The man who loved wages was made to announce the King whose sceptre no money could buy. But he saw the star from far off and died among the enemies of the people it would rise over (Numbers 31:8). To see Christ and not love him is the deepest madness of all.

The mercy in the road. The angel stood in the road with a drawn sword, and the donkey turned aside three times and saved Balaam’s life (Numbers 22:33). God often puts such obstacles in our way: a closed door, a rebuke, an illness, a word from an unexpected mouth. Do we beat the donkey or listen to it?

What it does not mean. Not that all who are paid for ministry are like Balaam; workers deserve their wages (1 Timothy 5:18). The sin is loving money and compromising truth for it.

In everyday life. A bank statement can be read as a spiritual document: what does yours say you love?

How do I know whether I love money too much? Would I compromise truth or conscience to keep or gain it? Do I give gladly or grudgingly? Does the thought of losing it fill me with fear? Does it shape my decisions more than God’s word? Do I resent those who have more? Love of money is a root of all kinds of evils (1 Timothy 6:10), and it hides well, especially in religious people. The cure is not only to hold it loosely but to love something better: to find Christ so satisfying that money returns to its place as a tool, not a god.

Textual note. Most manuscripts, followed by the KJV, call Balaam’s father Bosor, a variant form of the name; a few early ones read Beor, as in Numbers.
verseByVerse.note: Balaam was hired to curse Israel for money, and his donkey spoke to rebuke him.

verseByVerse.quote: These are waterless springs and mists driven by a storm. For them the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved. For, speaking loud boasts of folly, they entice by sensual passions of the flesh those who are barely escaping from those who live in error. They promise them freedom, but they themselves are slaves of corruption. For whatever overcomes a person, to that he is enslaved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The false teachers promise refreshment and freedom but give neither, because they are themselves enslaved to what they sell.

Waterless springs. A spring that promises water and gives none: in that dry country, a danger to life. God complained through Jeremiah that his people had forsaken him, the fountain of living waters, for broken cisterns that can hold no water (Jeremiah 2:13). False teachers are such cisterns.

Mists driven by a storm. Clouds that raise the farmer’s hope and pass over without rain (Jude 12).

The gloom of utter darkness. Their destiny is outer darkness (Matthew 8:12; 22:13; Jude 13). Reserved (tetērētai) is the custody word of verses 4 and 9. There is a grim fitness: men who promised light are held in the dark.

Loud boasts of folly. Swelling, bombastic words (hyperonka) full of emptiness (mataiotēs, Romans 8:20): as empty as a drum, and confidently delivered. And the bait is not an argument but appetite.

Barely escaping. Only a little escaping (oligōs apopheugontas): new converts just out of paganism, who broke with a way of life at real cost and are now told they need not have bothered.

They promise them freedom. Probably a twisted Christian freedom: grace means freedom from moral rules (Galatians 5:13; 1 Peter 2:16; Romans 6:1–2). It is the oldest lie in the world, the serpent’s promise in the garden: throw off God’s word and your eyes will be opened.

Slaves of corruption. Corruption is the moral decay of 1:4. Peter called himself a slave of Christ (1:1); these men, who promise freedom, are slaves of rot.

The fountain they counterfeit. Christ is the spring the false teachers imitate: on the last day of the feast he stood up and cried out, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37).

Whatever overcomes a person. Overcomes (hēttētai) is a battlefield word: the conquered become slaves (Romans 6:16). The man who throws off restraint has changed owners, and taken a worse one. Jesus said it first, and gave the only way out: everyone who practises sin is a slave to sin, and if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed (John 8:34–36). He breaks the old master’s hold at the cost of his own life, and takes his freed people under a yoke that is easy (Matthew 11:29–30).

What does real Christian freedom look like? Freedom from the guilt of sin, because Christ has paid for it; from its power, because we are united to him; from the law as a way of earning acceptance; and from the fear of death and judgment. But it is freedom for something: to love God and serve others (Galatians 5:13). A train is free on its rails and helpless off them; a fish is free in water and dies on the bank. We are free when we live as we were made to live, under the gentle rule of Christ.

I have just come to faith and feel shaky. How do I avoid being lured? Stay close to the flock and to faithful shepherds; predators pick off the sheep that wander alone. Join a Bible-teaching church and attend faithfully, read Scripture daily, starting with a Gospel, and find an older believer to meet with. Be wary of anyone who says the sins you have left were not so bad, or that grace means you need not change. When temptation comes dressed as freedom, ask where it leads.

Textual note. The KJV’s “clean escaped” follows later manuscripts with a word meaning truly, in place of “barely”.

verseByVerse.quote: For if, after they have escaped the defilements of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, the last state has become worse for them than the first. For it would have been better for them never to have known the way of righteousness than after knowing it to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them. What the true proverb says has happened to them: "The dog returns to its own vomit, and the sow, after washing herself, returns to wallow in the mire."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who turn back to the world after knowing Christ end worse off than if they had never known him, and their return shows they were washed but never changed.

After they have escaped. Among the most sobering verses in the New Testament. “They” are the false teachers, and perhaps those they led astray. Escaped is the word of 1:4: so far as anyone could see, they had left their former life and known the gospel, perhaps professed it.

Again entangled and overcome. Entangled (emplakentes) is woven in, like a fish in a net; overcome is the word of verse 19: conquered again by the master they once escaped.

The last state worse than the first. Peter echoes his Master’s words about a house swept clean and reoccupied by seven worse spirits (Matthew 12:45; Luke 11:26). Having known the truth and rejected it, they are more guilty and more hardened than before.

Better never to have known. The plain sense should not be blunted: greater knowledge brings greater responsibility (Luke 12:47–48; Hebrews 6:4–6; 10:26–29). The holy commandment is the Christian faith and way of life, delivered by the apostles (Jude 3). It was handed to them, and they put it down.

The true proverb. How does this stand with the perseverance of the saints, the teaching that those God truly saves he keeps to the end? Peter himself supplies the answer, and it is why the proverbs are there. The dog returns to its own vomit (Proverbs 26:11): it gets rid of what was making it sick, then goes back to it, because it is still a dog.

The sow, after washing herself. A popular proverb. The sow has been washed, genuinely and visibly; what she has not been given is a different nature. Washing a pig does not make it a sheep. That is Peter’s verdict: not that they lost salvation, but that they were cleaned rather than changed, which is what 1 John 2:19 says of those who went out from us because they were not of us.

Clean, but not every one of you. Peter had heard this distinction from the Lord himself, the night his own feet were washed: the one who has bathed is completely clean, “and you are clean, but not every one of you” (John 13:10). Judas had his feet washed by the hands of Christ, and went out into the night. Outward washing, even at Jesus’ hands, is not belonging to him. The cleansing that changes a nature is the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, poured out through Jesus Christ our Saviour (Titus 3:5–6).

The sheep returns to its Shepherd. The Lord Jesus does not wash pigs and leave them pigs. He gives a new heart and a new spirit, so that what we once loved becomes our grief, and what we once despised our joy. The dog returns to its vomit; the sheep returns to its Shepherd, because his is the voice it now loves, and no one will snatch it out of his hand.

In everyday life. The passage is meant to make believers not anxious but honest. Its question is not whether you have been washed but whether you have been changed, and the evidence is what you return to when you are tired, alone and unwatched. Thank God for every sign that you now love what you once hated; where the old pull remains, bring it to him today.

How can someone know so much and never be truly saved? Because knowing about Christ is not being united to him; Judas heard every sermon and saw every miracle. People can be moved by the gospel, reform their habits, join a church, even teach, and never have been born again (Matthew 7:21–23; 13:20–21). The difference is whether the Spirit gave a new heart, and the test is not how impressive a conversion looked but what a person keeps returning to over time.

I have gone back to an old sin. Am I the dog returning to its vomit? Not if you hate it and want to be free. The dog returns gladly, because it is what a dog loves. A child of God may fall back into sin, sometimes badly and repeatedly, but he is miserable there, confesses it, and longs to be clean (Psalm 51; 1 John 1:9). Peter himself denied Christ three times and was restored. If you are grieved, go to Christ today. He has not changed his mind about you, and the new nature in you is what makes the mud unbearable.

Where Christians differ: does this passage show that true believers can lose salvation? Arminian Christians, who hold that a true believer may finally turn away and be lost, read it so, pointing to “escaped” and to “the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ”. Many of them are earnest, godly believers, and the warning they stress is real. This commentary’s view: The proverbs answer the question. The dog and the sow returned to filth because their nature had never been changed; washed outwardly, they remained dogs and pigs. These people had outward knowledge of Christ and outward moral reform, but never received a new nature (1:4). True believers, made partakers of the divine nature, are kept by God’s power (1 Peter 1:5) and will never finally fall (1:10). Those who return permanently to their former life show they were never truly regenerated (1 John 2:19).

2.theology: The chapter’s great question is apostasy, falling away from the faith: can a person who has genuinely known Christ fall finally away? The Reformed answer is that those truly born again will persevere (John 10:28–29; Romans 8:38–39); how the dog and the sow show who those who fall away were is treated at vv. 20–22.
2.examples: The Balaam portrait (vv. 15–16) gives a congregation a plain test. What does this teacher gain from what he teaches? Balaam’s gift was real, but it became a commodity. The test of a ministry is not whether the gifts are real but whether the teacher loves the Lord more than the wages.

keyVerse.quote: then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials, and to keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment,
keyVerse.note: This is where the long sentence of verses 4–9 lands, and it holds the chapter’s two threads together: judgment on the false teachers and rescue for the godly. Peter does not ask his readers to work out how God will act; it is enough that he knows how, as he showed with Noah and Lot, and above all at the cross.

2.reflection:
Peter says the false teachers “secretly bring in” their errors alongside the truth (v. 1). Why is error added to the truth harder to spot than error that openly replaces it? Where do you see that happening today?

Peter gives three tests of a teacher: what he does with Christ, how he lives, and what he wants from his hearers (vv. 1–3, 14–15). How could you use those tests, fairly and humbly, with the preachers, books and podcasts you listen to?

Lot is called “righteous” three times despite his record, and the evidence Peter gives is his distress at the evil around him (vv. 7–8). What comfort, and what warning, does his story hold for a believer who lives or works somewhere hard?

The false teachers promise freedom but are slaves (v. 19), and the washed sow goes back to the mire (v. 22). What is the difference between being cleaned up and being made new, and what does it show you about real Christian freedom?

3.title: The Day That Is Coming
3.overview:
Where we are. The last chapter is the letter’s goal. Chapter 2 exposed the false teachers; now Peter answers the claim that made their way of life feel safe: that Christ is not coming back.

The message. Christ will come, as surely as God’s word made the world and once judged it; and the delay is not slowness but patience, holding the door open for repentance. So the question is not “When?” but “What sort of people ought you to be?” Live now as people bound for new heavens and a new earth where righteousness will be at home.

Why it was said. The scoffers argued that nothing ever changes: the first generation had died, the world ran on as it always had, so there was no judgment to fear and no reason to restrain desire (see the introduction). Peter, soon to die himself (1:14), wants his readers forewarned and steady after he has gone.

How the chapter makes its case. Verses 1–2 call the readers back to the prophets and apostles. Verses 3–4 quote the scoffers and name their real motive. Then come three answers: the world has not always continued as it was, for God’s word made it, flooded it, and keeps it now for fire (vv. 5–7); God does not reckon time as we do (v. 8); and the delay is patience, “not wishing that any should perish” (v. 9). Yet the day will come like a thief and lay everything bare (v. 10). So believers are to live holy lives, waiting for and hastening that day and the new world beyond it (vv. 11–13); to be found spotless and at peace, counting the Lord’s patience as salvation, as Paul also wrote (vv. 14–16); and, forewarned, to stand firm and keep growing (vv. 17–18).

Where it leads. The promise the scoffers mock is Jesus’ own, and the empty tomb pledges it: the one whose promise to rise was mocked and kept will keep his promise to return. The patience that delays the end is his, the patience that waited for a persecutor on the Damascus road and for a disciple who denied him. And the letter closes, unusually, by giving Jesus Christ the glory that belongs to God alone, “both now and to the day of eternity”.

For us. Every sunrise is another day of his patience, and another day nearer his coming. Use it: deal with what you would hurry to hide, pray for those not yet home, read Scripture humbly, and keep growing in the grace and knowledge of the Lord who will bring a world where righteousness is finally at home.
