In both of them I am stirring up your sincere mind by way of reminder,<sup>2</sup>that you should remember the predictions of the holy prophets and the commandment of the Lord and Savior through your apostles,<sup>3</sup>knowing this first of all, that scoffers will come in the last days with scoffing, following their own sinful desires.<sup>4</sup>They will say, "Where is the promise of his coming? For ever since the fathers fell asleep, all things are continuing as they were from the beginning of creation."<sup>5</sup>For they deliberately overlook this fact, that the heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God,<sup>6</sup>and that by means of these the world that then existed was deluged with water and perished.<sup>7</sup>But by the same word the heavens and earth that now exist are stored up for fire, being kept until the day of judgment and destruction of the ungodly.<sup>8</sup>But do not overlook this one fact, beloved, that with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.<sup>9</sup>The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.<sup>10</sup>But the day of the Lord will come like a thief, and then the heavens will pass away with a roar, and the heavenly bodies will be burned up and dissolved, and the earth and the works that are done on it will be exposed.<sup>11</sup>Since all these things are thus to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in lives of holiness and godliness,<sup>12</sup>waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of God, because of which the heavens will be set on fire and dissolved, and the heavenly bodies will melt as they burn!<sup>13</sup>But according to his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells.<sup>14</sup>Therefore, beloved, since you are waiting for these, be diligent to be found by him without spot or blemish, and at peace.<sup>15</sup>And count the patience of our Lord as salvation, just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote to you according to the wisdom given him,<sup>16</sup>as he does in all his letters when he speaks in them of these matters. There are some things in them that are hard to understand, which the ignorant and unstable twist to their own destruction, as they do the other Scriptures.<sup>17</sup>You therefore, beloved, knowing this beforehand, take care that you are not carried away with the error of lawless people and lose your own stability.<sup>18</sup>But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Scoffers and the Day
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The world will not go on for ever as it is: Christ will come, and the delay is God’s patience. Peter recalls his readers to the prophets and apostles (vv. 1–2) and warns that scoffers, driven by their desires, will mock the promise because nothing seems to change (vv. 3–4). He answers that God’s word created the world, judged it by water and keeps it for fire (vv. 5–7); that God does not reckon time as we do (v. 8); and that the delay is patience, giving time for repentance (v. 9). But the day will come like a thief, and everything done on the earth will be laid bare (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology:
Not Slowness but Patience

The world has not always continued as it was: God’s word made it and judged it by the flood. The Lord is not slow but patient, and the day will come like a thief.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Scoffers pointed to the death of the first generation as proof that nothing was coming.

Now: The delay is mercy; the right response is repentance, not argument about the timetable.

verseByVerse.quote: This is now the second letter that I am writing to you, beloved. In both of them I am stirring up your sincere mind by way of reminder, that you should remember the predictions of the holy prophets and the commandment of the Lord and Savior through your apostles,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter writes to rouse sincere believers to remember what the prophets foretold and the apostles taught, for that memory is their defence against the scoffers.

The second letter. The earlier letter is most likely 1 Peter. Beloved (agapētoi) comes four times in this chapter (vv. 1, 8, 14, 17), a warm contrast with the hard words about false teachers.

Stirring up your sincere mind. Stirring up (diegeirō) is the waking verb again from 1:13: his readers do not need new material; they need rousing. Sincere (eilikrinē) means pure, unmixed. Peter credits them with genuineness even as he warns them, for even a sincere mind can grow drowsy.

The predictions of the holy prophets. The Old Testament prophets foretold the Day of the Lord, judgment and new creation (Isaiah 65:17; 66:22; Joel 2; Daniel 7; 12). Remembering them is the defence against the scoffers who follow.

Through your apostles. The commandment is the apostolic teaching, including Christ’s promise to return, and they are your apostles: not a distant institution but the men who actually brought them the gospel. Prophets and apostles stand side by side, equal in weight (compare v. 16; Ephesians 2:20).

One Person. Both point to him. The risen Lord opened his disciples’ minds to see that everything written about him in the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled (Luke 24:44–45). The prophets foretold him, the apostles were sent by him, and the commandment is his own.

In everyday life. Pick one promise of Christ’s return and read it each morning this week: Acts 1:11, John 14:3, or Isaiah 65:17–25. And thank God for whoever first brought you the apostles’ message.

Why does it matter that the prophets and apostles are put together? Because the whole Bible speaks with one voice and one authority. The Old Testament is not outdated, and the New is not merely the church’s opinion about Jesus. The day of the Lord in Joel or Zephaniah and in Peter is one story from one Author, promised in the one and explained in the other; read them together.
verseByVerse.note: The earlier letter is most likely 1 Peter.

verseByVerse.quote: knowing this first of all, that scoffers will come in the last days with scoffing, following their own sinful desires. They will say, "Where is the promise of his coming? For ever since the fathers fell asleep, all things are continuing as they were from the beginning of creation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Scoffers who mock Christ’s return were foretold, and their mockery springs from their desires more than from their arguments. Their case is that nothing ever changes.

Scoffers will come in the last days. Knowing this first of all, as in 1:20: before you hear the scoffers, know that they were foretold. Scoffers with scoffing (empaiktai en empaigmonē) is a Hebrew way of adding emphasis, and every scoffer is, without meaning to be, a fulfilled prophecy. The last days are the whole period since Christ’s first coming (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2; Jude 18).

Following their own sinful desires. Peter names the motive before the argument. Their doctrine has a cause, and the cause is not intellectual: if there is no coming judgment, there is no reason to restrain oneself. He is describing these particular mockers, not saying that every honest doubter is hiding a sin.

Where is the promise of his coming? The taunt itself. The promise of his coming (hē epangelia tēs parousias autou) is Jesus’ promise to return (John 14:3; Acts 1:11). The question echoes Old Testament scoffers, who asked the psalmist all the day long where his God was (Psalm 42:3), and asked, “Where is the God of justice?” (Malachi 2:17).

Ever since the fathers fell asleep. Fell asleep (ekoimēthēsan), a common Christian word for dying (1 Thessalonians 4:13–15), already carries the hope of waking. (It describes the body; the soul is with Christ, Philippians 1:23.) The argument has two parts, and this is the first: the fathers had died, and nothing had happened, a real problem in a church burying its founders (see “Uncertain wording” below).

All things are continuing as they were. The second part argues from the world’s sameness: nature has always run on unchanged, so God does not step in. It sounds very modern. Peter does not dispute that the sun rises every morning; he disputes the conclusion, pointing to two occasions when things did not continue as they were (vv. 5–6). The Lord who made all things and raised his Son from the tomb is not bound by the regularity he himself sustains. Every sunrise is his faithfulness, and brings his coming a day nearer.

The promise was his own. The scoffers are mocking not a church doctrine but the word of Jesus: “I will come again and will take you to myself” (John 14:3). His promises had been mocked before. At the cross the chief priests jeered, “He saved others; he cannot save himself” (Matthew 27:42), and afterwards called him the impostor who had said he would rise after three days (Matthew 27:63). On the third day the tomb was empty. The promise to rise was mocked and kept, and that pledges the promise to return: God has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead (Acts 17:31).

In everyday life. Is there any area of your life where you live as though he were not coming, because you would rather he did not see it yet? Bring it into the light today; he who is coming forgives all who confess (1 John 1:9).

Is it wrong to wonder why Christ has not yet come? No. Honest questions are not scoffing: the souls under the altar cry, how long? (Revelation 6:10), and the psalms are full of it. Peter condemns mocking unbelief that uses the delay as an excuse to live as one pleases. The scoffer asks where is he? hoping the answer is nowhere; the believer asks because he longs to see him, and his question is a kind of prayer: come, Lord Jesus.

How should I answer someone who says the world just runs by natural laws? Agree that the world is wonderfully regular, and ask why. Its regularity is evidence of God’s faithful upholding of all things by the word of his power (Hebrews 1:3; Genesis 8:22). Laws describe how things normally go; they do not forbid the Lawgiver to act. And history is not a closed loop: it had a beginning, it has seen a resurrection, and it is moving toward an end. Be gentle, and point the conversation to Jesus’ resurrection, the decisive interruption.

Uncertain wording. Who “the fathers” are is not certain: probably the first generation of Christians, or perhaps the Old Testament patriarchs. Many scholars take the first reading as a sign that the letter was written after the apostles’ generation, and so after Peter. But by the mid-60s many first believers had died, Stephen and James among them; and if the fathers are the patriarchs, the phrase says nothing about date at all.

verseByVerse.quote: For they deliberately overlook this fact, that the heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God, and that by means of these the world that then existed was deluged with water and perished. But by the same word the heavens and earth that now exist are stored up for fire, being kept until the day of judgment and destruction of the ungodly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The world has not always continued as it was: God’s word made it, once destroyed it by water, and now keeps it for judgment by fire.

They deliberately overlook this fact. It escapes their notice because they want it to (lanthanei thelontas). Their ignorance is chosen (Romans 1:18–21).

By the word of God. The first fact they ignore: God made the world by his word (Genesis 1; Hebrews 11:3), and the earth emerged from the waters (Genesis 1:2, 6–10). Their claim collapses at its own word “creation”: a created world has not always been as it is.

Deluged with water and perished. The second fact: the flood. Deluged (kataklystheis) gives us cataclysm. The water the world was formed through later destroyed it, at the word of God, in Scriptures the scoffers claim to respect.

By the same word. One word made it, flooded it, and holds it now: the world is held steady by the same voice that could end it. Stored up (tethēsaurismenoi) is treasured up. The next judgment will be by fire, not water: God promised Noah never again to destroy the earth by a flood (Genesis 9:11), and the prophets speak of fire (Isaiah 66:15–16; Malachi 4:1; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–8).

Being kept until the day of judgment. Kept (tēroumenoi) is the custody word again, as of the angels in 2:4. The universe is not a machine running down but something held in reserve. Destruction (apōleia) is ruin: for the ungodly, eternal ruin.

The Word who holds it. This word is a Person. All things were made through the eternal Word (John 1:3), and the Son upholds the universe by the word of his power (Hebrews 1:3): he spoke, and the dry land appeared; he spoke again, and the deep broke open; he speaks still, and the earth keeps its seasons. The world is kept for judgment by the Lord who will be revealed in flaming fire (2 Thessalonians 1:7–8), and kept for mercy by the Son who came the first time not to condemn the world but to save it (John 3:17). For his people the coming fire holds no terror: he has already borne in his own body the wrath their sins had stored up.

What it does not mean. Destruction does not mean annihilation of the ungodly. Scripture describes their punishment as eternal and conscious (Matthew 25:46; Revelation 14:11; 20:10); the word means ruin, the loss of all that makes existence good. Some evangelical Christians hold that the lost will finally cease to exist; this commentary respects them but holds the historic view, chiefly because Jesus sets eternal punishment beside eternal life in the same sentence (Matthew 25:46).

Was the flood worldwide? Genesis describes a flood that covered all the high mountains under the whole heaven (Genesis 7:19), and Peter sets it beside the judgment of the whole earth by fire. Most Christians have read it as worldwide; some godly scholars hold that it covered the whole inhabited region. Either way it was a real judgment, and Noah’s rescue a real salvation.

Should a Christian fear that the world will end in a nuclear war or climate disaster? We should care for God’s creation and work for peace, as stewards of what he made. But the heavens and earth are kept by his word for his day, and history will end not by accident or by our hand, but when and as he has appointed. That frees us both from despair and from thinking we must save the planet ourselves. Do your duty calmly, and trust the Keeper.

Uncertain wording. Two phrases are compressed. Formed “out of water and through water” (v. 5) probably recalls Genesis 1, where dry land appeared from the waters and was shaped by their parting. “By means of these” (v. 6) is plural: perhaps the water and the word together, or the waters above and below that broke out in the flood (Genesis 7:11). Either way, the world that came out of water was undone by water, at God’s word.

verseByVerse.quote: But do not overlook this one fact, beloved, that with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God does not measure time as we do, so the long delay the scoffers mock is no delay to him. Yet no single day is small in his sight.

Do not overlook this one fact. The verb of verse 5, turned round: the scoffers deliberately forget; believers must not.

One day is as a thousand years. The line echoes Psalm 90:4: a thousand years in your sight are but as yesterday when it is past. To a creature with seventy or eighty years, a delay of two millennia seems decisive; to the One who made time it is not a delay at all. The scoffers’ argument depends entirely on assuming God experiences time as they do.

Both halves are needed. The comparison runs both ways, so it cannot be used to calculate dates. A thousand years as one day: the long wait is nothing to him. One day as a thousand years: no single day is trivial to him, and he gives each day of your life the attention of a thousand years. Our years are a breath to him, and yet he numbers our hairs and counts our tears.

The Lord of the thousand years. Peter’s Lord is not a distant clock-keeper. The one for whom a thousand years are as a day is the Son who could say, before Abraham was, I am (John 8:58), and who then lived some thirty years of ordinary days in Nazareth before his hour came. The eternal Son entered time, so the one who delays knows from the inside what waiting is. And if any single day has carried the weight of a thousand years, it was the day he said, it is finished (John 19:30).

Why would God make his people wait so long? Peter gives the main answer in the next verse: patience, so that more may repent. But waiting is also how God grows faith. Abraham waited twenty-five years for Isaac; Israel waited centuries for the Messiah. In the waiting God refines his people, teaches them to walk by faith, and gathers in his elect. The wait is long to us, but not empty.

Does this mean that the days of creation were long ages? This verse does not say so. Peter is explaining the delay of Christ’s coming, not offering a conversion table, and reading it as one has caused much confusion. The days of Genesis 1 must be read from Genesis itself, and read there they are six ordinary days: each is numbered and closed with evening and morning, and the fourth commandment grounds our working week in God’s six days of making (Exodus 20:11). This commentary holds that God made all things in six ordinary days and, with the genealogies of Genesis, that the creation is young. Other faithful Christians read the days as long ages, as a literary framework, or as God’s workdays described by analogy with ours, often weighing the evidence for an old earth or the careful shape of the chapter; they deserve a patient hearing, and all agree that God made all things by his word. Whatever view one takes, this verse does not settle it, because it is not about creation.

Where Christians differ: does this verse teach a thousand-year day or a millennial scheme? Some have used it to calculate the timing of Christ’s return, such as six thousand years of history followed by a thousand-year millennium. This commentary’s view: The verse is not a formula for calculation; it teaches that God’s perspective on time differs from ours. It warns against date-setting rather than encouraging it (Matthew 24:36; Acts 1:7), and gives no support to millennial timetables. (Christians differ on the thousand years of Revelation 20 itself, whether a future earthly reign of Christ or his present reign from heaven; this verse does not decide that question.)

parallels.desc: a thousand years in your sight are but as yesterday

verseByVerse.quote: The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The delay is not slowness but patience: the Lord is holding back the end so that people may repent.

Not slow to fulfill his promise. Slow (bradynei) is to loiter. It only looks like slowness to those who judge him by their own clock.

But is patient toward you. The heart of the chapter. Patient (makrothymei) is literally long of temper, slow to anger. Toward you: God’s beloved people (v. 1), the chosen (1 Peter 1:1). The scoffers treated the interval as evidence against God; it is evidence of his mercy, the very mercy that is sparing them.

Not wishing that any should perish. God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 18:23, 32; 33:11), and his patience gives time for repentance (metanoia), a change of mind and direction (Romans 2:4).

What it means to come to repentance. Most of us hear “repent” as a threat, so a God who waits for repentance can sound like a headmaster tapping his watch. Peter turns that round: the waiting is love making room. To repent is to turn: to stop running your life on your own terms, own that you were wrong, and come back to God, beneath the wrong deeds to what we were trusting instead of him. Timothy Keller often pointed out that if you think God accepts you because of your performance, repentance will feel like a threat, and you will avoid it; but if you know you are accepted in Christ, it becomes a relief, even a joy, because nothing you confess can overturn his verdict. And Christ gives it: “God exalted him at his right hand as Leader and Savior, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins” (Acts 5:31). When you see a sin this week, do not hide it or explain it away; name it to him and come home. See also Repentance in the Theological Dictionary.

The patience of our Lord. Peter will tell them to count the patience of our Lord as salvation (v. 15), and the New Testament shows that patience with a human face. Paul, once a persecutor, wrote that he received mercy so that in him, the foremost of sinners, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who would believe (1 Timothy 1:15–16). It is the patience of the Saviour who wept over Jerusalem, prayed for those who crucified him, and reigns now while the last of his sheep are gathered in. He waited for the thief on the cross and for the persecutor on the Damascus road, and he waited for us.

The use of the verse. However Christians explain it (see below), the verse never allows what the scoffers wanted, that the delay means nothing is coming. If God is holding the door open, anyone still outside should not argue about how it works but walk through.

If God has chosen his elect, why should I evangelise? Because God has chosen the means as well as the end: the elect are brought to repentance through the gospel preached (Romans 10:14–17), and God waits so that it may reach them. Paul was told to keep speaking in Corinth because the Lord had many people in that city (Acts 18:9–10). You do not know who the elect are, so offer Christ freely and sincerely to everyone, as God himself does. Every day of patience is a day for the gospel.

I have a loved one who has not repented. Is it too late? Not while they are alive, and not while the Lord is patient. God waited for you, perhaps for years, and he knows how to bring the hardest heart to repentance, as he did with Saul of Tarsus. Pray specifically, live kindly before them, speak of Christ when doors open, and leave the timing with God. His patience is room being made for repentance.

Where Christians differ: if God wishes all to repent, why are not all saved? Arminians read this verse as showing that God wills every individual to be saved and that human choice makes the difference; universalists as showing that all will eventually be saved. Both Reformed and Arminian Christians want to honour God’s mercy. This commentary’s view: The context helps: God is patient toward you, the beloved, the elect. Christ’s return is delayed so that all God’s people, including those not yet converted, may come to repentance; when the last of the elect is brought in, he will return. At the same time, Scripture teaches that God sincerely desires the repentance of all sinners, in that he delights in repentance and offers the gospel freely to all (Ezekiel 33:11; 1 Timothy 2:4), while he has also sovereignly chosen to save some and not all. These two truths, God’s revealed desire and his decreed purpose, are both taught and must both be held. Universalism contradicts the next verse and the clear teaching of eternal judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: But the day of the Lord will come like a thief, and then the heavens will pass away with a roar, and the heavenly bodies will be burned up and dissolved, and the earth and the works that are done on it will be exposed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The day of the Lord will come suddenly and unmistakably, dissolving the present order and laying bare everything done on the earth.

Like a thief. The day of the Lord is the Old Testament term for God’s great day of judgment and salvation (Joel 2:31; Amos 5:18–20; Zephaniah 1:14–18), now identified with Christ’s return. The thief image is the Lord’s own (Matthew 24:43; 1 Thessalonians 5:2). The point is not stealth but surprise, for this thief does not come quietly: the heavens will roar. The scoffers asked where the promise was; the promise includes the fact that you will not see it coming.

With a roar. Pass away (pareleusontai) is the word Jesus used: heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away (Matthew 24:35). With a roar (rhoizēdon) imitates a rushing noise, like the crackle of a great fire.

Burned up and dissolved. Dissolved (lythēsetai) is the word for untying something. The heavens that declare the glory of God will roar at his coming, and the stars that have kept their courses since the beginning will be loosed by the hand that set them.

Will be exposed. The most important clause. Exposed (heurethēsetai) is will be found, laid bare: not mere destruction but disclosure. The fire is not chiefly an incinerator but a searchlight. Everything done on this earth will be brought into the open before God’s judgment (1 Corinthians 3:13; Hebrews 4:13). Peter’s point against men living as they pleased is not only that the world will end but that it will be examined.

Eyes like a flame of fire. The eyes that see it will be Christ’s: we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10), whose eyes are like a flame of fire (Revelation 1:14). That is hard news for a heart that lives for its reputation, because on that day what other people thought of us will count for nothing. And it is good news for anyone wronged in secret and never vindicated: on that day the truth will come out.

In everyday life. If Christ came today, what would be exposed in your life? Christ has already borne what the fire would find, so this is not terror; but deal with the thing you would hurry to hide, and you will say more easily, come, Lord Jesus.

If he comes like a thief, does that not mean a secret coming? No. The thief image describes the timing, not the manner. The same Lord said his coming would be like lightning flashing from east to west (Matthew 24:27), and every eye will see him (Revelation 1:7); here the thief’s arrival comes with the roar of the heavens. Sudden for everyone, secret to no one: believers need not fear a silent disappearance, but must be ready at any hour for a return that will fill the sky.

Will the earth then be annihilated, or renewed? Some Christians hold that the old creation will be destroyed and replaced, pointing to pass away and dissolved. But Peter compares it to the flood, which cleansed the world rather than abolishing it (v. 6), and says the earth will be exposed; and Paul says creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption (Romans 8:21). The more likely reading is that the present creation will be purged by fire and renewed.

Should I try to work out when it will happen? No. No one knows the day or the hour (Matthew 24:36), nor the times the Father has fixed (Acts 1:7), and every attempt to set dates has failed and brought the faith into ridicule. The signs Jesus gave (wars, false teachers, persecution, the gospel to the nations) mark the whole age, so that every generation should be ready. Scripture names things that come first, the gospel preached to all nations (Matthew 24:14) and the man of lawlessness revealed (2 Thessalonians 2:1–4); so his coming is near and always to be expected, yet never to be dated. Do not calculate the hour; keep the house ready at all hours.

Where Christians differ: is the day of the Lord a single event? Dispensationalists (who see God’s plan in distinct stages, with separate futures for Israel and the church) often separate a secret rapture of the church from a later visible return, and place a thousand-year earthly kingdom between Christ’s return and the final judgment and new creation. Other premillennialists, rejecting a secret rapture, still see a sequence: return, thousand-year reign, then final judgment and new creation. This commentary’s view: Peter places Christ’s coming, the day of the Lord, the judgment of the ungodly and the dissolution of the present heavens and earth together in one great event, followed by the new heavens and new earth (vv. 7, 10, 12–13). This fits the amillennial understanding (that the thousand years of Revelation 20 describe Christ’s present reign, not a later earthly kingdom): one visible return of Christ, at which the dead are raised, all are judged, and creation is renewed, with no secret rapture and no intervening earthly millennium. Many faithful Christians hold premillennial or dispensational views and share the hope this chapter teaches: Christ is coming, visibly and in glory, and his people must be ready. This commentary differs from them on the order of events, not on the hope.

Uncertain wording. Heavenly bodies translates stoicheia, “elements”, whose meaning here is uncertain: the basic elements of the physical world, or the sun, moon and stars (compare Isaiah 34:4). The ESV follows the second, which suits the mention of the heavens just before. Either way the dissolution of the present order is total.

Textual note. The manuscripts differ at the end of this verse. The oldest read will be found or exposed (heurethēsetai); later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read will be burned up (katakaēsetai); some read will not be found. “Will be found” is the harder reading, and so most likely original, meaning laid bare before God’s judgment.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–18 — New Heavens, and the Last Command
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because the present world is passing and a new one is promised, God’s people should live now as citizens of the world to come. Peter turns the coming dissolution into a question of character: holy and godly lives, waiting for and hastening the day, and looking for new heavens and a new earth where righteousness is at home (vv. 11–13). So be found spotless and at peace, and count the Lord’s patience as salvation, as Paul also taught in letters some twist (vv. 14–16). Forewarned, do not be swept away, but keep growing in the grace and knowledge of Christ, to whom belongs the glory for ever (vv. 17–18).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Answer to Error Is Growth

Since everything will be laid bare, live in holiness and godliness while waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells. The last command is to grow in the grace and knowledge of Christ.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter called Paul a beloved brother and counted his letters among the Scriptures.

Now: A growing believer is far harder to uproot than one who is merely on guard.

verseByVerse.quote: Since all these things are thus to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in lives of holiness and godliness, waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of God, because of which the heavens will be set on fire and dissolved, and the heavenly bodies will melt as they burn! But according to his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because this world is passing and God has promised a new one, his people should live holy and godly lives now, eagerly waiting for that day.

All these things are thus to be dissolved. As good as dissolving already: the Greek is present tense. Everything you can see has a date stamped on it that you cannot read.

What sort of people ought you to be. Not speculation, date-setting or withdrawal: the question is about character. Holiness (hagiais anastrophais) is holy ways of life, plural: in every area. It is belonging to God and becoming like him (1 Peter 1:15). Godliness is plural too: godly acts, not a mood. Teaching about the last things is given to change how we live, not to feed curiosity (1 John 3:2–3). If the house is to be pulled down, you do not spend your life polishing its brass; you invest in what will last.

Waiting for and hastening. Waiting (prosdokōntas) is looking eagerly, as a family watches the road for a returning son. Hastening (speudontas) ordinarily means to speed something up. Since the delay is God’s patience, believers can in some sense hasten the day: by holy living, by prayer (your kingdom come, Matthew 6:10), and by evangelism, which brings in those whose conversion the Lord awaits (v. 9; Matthew 24:14). That is a dignity given to ordinary obedience.

Will melt as they burn! The description is bleak, until verse 13 turns it round. Melt (tēketai), as in the Greek of Isaiah 34:4, and Micah 1:4, where the mountains melt under the LORD like wax before the fire.

New heavens and a new earth. The point of the passage, and his promise (Isaiah 65:17; 66:22): the scoffers asked, where is the promise? Here it is. New (kainous) suggests new in quality: not another universe replacing this one, but this one transformed (Revelation 21:1–5; Romans 8:19–21), a physical world set free, with resurrected people in resurrected bodies.

In which righteousness dwells. Dwells (katoikei) is settles down, makes its permanent home. Here righteousness is a visitor often turned away at the door; there it will be at home, with no more sin, injustice or death (Revelation 21:4, 27). That answers the men of chapter 2, who seemed to get away with their sin.

The fire is not the end. Righteousness at home means the Righteous One at home among his people: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man” (Revelation 21:3). The Lord who was a stranger in his own world, with no home of his own in it, will dwell with them for ever, and wipe away every tear with his own hand.

What it does not mean. Hastening does not mean we control God’s timetable or can force his hand. It means God uses his people’s prayers, holiness and witness in bringing about his purposes.

In everyday life. Pray your kingdom come, and mean it: the Spirit, God’s pledge of that new world, already lives in you. Then choose one concrete act of holiness today: an apology, an honest word, a gift, a conversation about Christ. Each is a brick in a house that will not burn.

What will the new heavens and new earth actually be like? Scripture gives glimpses rather than a map, but they are glorious. A real, physical world, this creation renewed, as our risen bodies will be these bodies glorified (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). God dwelling with his people, and no more tears, death, mourning or pain (Revelation 21:3–4). Work without frustration, worship without weariness, fellowship without sin, the glory of the nations brought in (Revelation 21:24–26). Above all, we will see his face (Revelation 22:4). Whatever is good in this world will be there, freed from the curse, and Christ will be its light.

If this world will be dissolved, does it matter what I do with it now? Yes. The new creation is this creation renewed, so work done in the Lord is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58): caring for creation, doing justice, raising children, making things well, healing the sick. What will not survive is sin, and whatever was done for self rather than for God (1 Corinthians 3:12–15). Hold this world loosely, because it is passing, and serve it diligently, because it is his.

Uncertain wording. Hastening (speudontas) can also mean “earnestly desiring”, and some translations take it so. The usual sense, to hurry something on, fits verse 9 well; but either is possible, and both describe hearts set on Christ’s coming.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, beloved, since you are waiting for these, be diligent to be found by him without spot or blemish, and at peace. And count the patience of our Lord as salvation, just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote to you according to the wisdom given him, as he does in all his letters when he speaks in them of these matters. There are some things in them that are hard to understand, which the ignorant and unstable twist to their own destruction, as they do the other Scriptures.
verseByVerse.commentary:
People waiting for that world should be diligent to be found pure and at peace, and should count the Lord’s delay as salvation, as Paul also taught in letters that are Scripture, though some twist them.

Since you are waiting for these. People who expect a wedding prepare for it.

Without spot or blemish, and at peace. Be diligent (spoudasate) is the letter’s word for earnest, grace-driven effort (1:5, 10). Found (heurethēnai) picks up verse 10: everything will be found out, so be diligent about what is found in you. Without spot or blemish: like Christ, the spotless Lamb (1 Peter 1:19), and the opposite of the false teachers, blots and blemishes at the church’s own feast (2:13). At peace: with God through Christ (Romans 5:1), and with one another.

Count the patience of our Lord as salvation. This turns verse 9 into a command. The scoffers count it slowness; believers count it salvation. Every day Christ has not yet come is another day in which someone you love can still turn to him, and in which you yourself are being made ready (v. 14).

Our beloved brother Paul. These two men had a serious public disagreement at Antioch, where Paul opposed Peter to his face and later told the story in a letter the churches read (Galatians 2:11–14). Peter calls him beloved brother and commends his wisdom as given him by God. Paul also taught that God’s patience leads to repentance (Romans 2:4).

That is what grace does to an old wound. There is no trace of the quarrel. The Lord’s patience saved the apostle who denied him and the apostle who persecuted him, and made the two of them beloved brothers who wrote, by the wisdom God gave them, the Scriptures we still read.

Hard to understand. An honest admission from one apostle about another, and a small comfort to anyone who has struggled through Romans. Some of Paul’s teaching, perhaps on grace, freedom, election or the last things, requires careful thought.

Twist to their own destruction. Ignorant (amatheis) is untaught; unstable (astēriktoi) is not established, as in 2:14. Twist (streblousin) is to wrench, as on a rack. The false teachers twisted Paul’s teaching on grace into a licence for immorality (Romans 3:8; 6:1). The hard passages are not to blame; the fault lies in untaught, unsteady readers, who twist the plain parts too.

The other Scriptures. Peter already counts Paul’s letters among the Scriptures. Many scholars see this as a sign of a later date, when Paul’s letters had been collected. But they were copied and passed between churches in his own lifetime (Colossians 4:16), and Peter speaks only of the letters he knows. If, as this commentary holds, Peter wrote this, Paul was very likely still alive or, if the early tradition of his death under Nero is right, only lately martyred. Either way, one New Testament writer already recognises another’s letters as Scripture.

What it does not mean. Not that Scripture is unclear in its main message, or that ordinary believers cannot read it (Psalm 19:7); some passages need careful, humble study.

In everyday life. Is there someone with whom you are not at peace, perhaps a fellow believer who once rebuked you publicly, as Paul did Peter? Christ has made your peace with God, so follow Peter’s example: speak of them warmly, and seek peace.

How can I be found without spot or blemish when I still sin? First, by standing in Christ: his spotless righteousness is counted as yours, and his blood cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7; Philippians 3:9). Second, by growing in holiness now, the fruit and evidence of being in him. Peter calls for diligence, not perfection: keep short accounts with God, make peace with those you have wronged, and pursue holiness from a heart at rest in Christ’s finished work. He will present you blameless (Jude 24).

How can I avoid twisting Scripture? Read whole passages, not isolated verses, and ask what the author meant to his first readers before asking what it means for you. Let clear passages interpret harder ones. Read with the church: good preaching, sound commentaries and the confessions keep you from private eccentricities. Be especially careful when an interpretation happens to excuse what you already wanted to do; that was the false teachers’ method. Come ready to be corrected by the Bible rather than to use it.

Uncertain wording. Which letter Peter means by “wrote to you” is not certain. He is writing to the same churches as 1 Peter (3:1), so it may be Galatians, Ephesians or Colossians, all sent to churches in those regions, or Paul’s teaching in general; Peter adds at once that all Paul’s letters say the same.
verseByVerse.note: Peter already counts Paul’s letters among “the Scriptures.”

verseByVerse.quote: You therefore, beloved, knowing this beforehand, take care that you are not carried away with the error of lawless people and lose your own stability. But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Forewarned, believers must guard against being swept away by error, and the way to stand firm is to keep growing in the grace and knowledge of Christ. The letter ends by giving Jesus the glory that belongs to God.

Knowing this beforehand. Being forewarned (proginōskontes): the letter’s purpose in a phrase. Forewarning is itself protection.

Take care that you are not carried away. Take care (phylassesthe) is a sentry’s word. Carried away (synapachthentes) is swept along, as by a crowd: the word Paul used of Barnabas being carried away by Peter’s hypocrisy at Antioch (Galatians 2:13). Peter knew from his own failure how easily a good man is swept along. Lawless (athesmōn) is the word used of the men of Sodom (2:7).

Lose your own stability. Stability (stērigmos) shares a root with established (1:12) and with the “unsteady” souls who are baited (2:14) and the “unstable” who twist Scripture (3:16). Peter’s fear is that the steady will be pulled into that instability. And it is the word Jesus gave him: when you have turned again, strengthen (stērison) your brothers (Luke 22:32). His last sentence is still obeying that command.

But grow in the grace and knowledge. After two chapters of warning, the last command is unexpected. Grow (auxanete) is present tense: keep growing. Peter does not end by telling them to watch the heretics more closely, but to get on with maturing; a growing tree is far harder to uproot than one propped up. Grace is God’s favour, known ever more deeply, for a man who forgets he was cleansed stops growing (1:9). Knowledge is personal knowledge of Christ (1:2–3, 8), reclaimed from the men peddling a counterfeit: the answer to false knowledge is not less knowledge but the real thing. The letter ends where it began (1:2).

To him be the glory. To Jesus Christ: a doxology offering him the glory due to God alone, who says, my glory I give to no other (Isaiah 42:8). The letter began by calling him our God and Saviour (1:1), and it ends by giving him God’s glory. Day of eternity (hēmera aiōnos) occurs nowhere else in the New Testament: a day that has no evening. If, as this commentary holds, Peter wrote them, these are his last recorded words, written when he knew his death was near.

That is what grace does. The last word of Peter is glory, and the glory is Christ’s. The fisherman who sank in the waves, who cursed and swore that he did not know him, who was found and forgiven on a beach at dawn, ends his life giving that same Lord the glory that belongs to God alone. To our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ be the glory, now, in the long patience of this age, and on the day of eternity that will never end. Amen.

What it does not mean. Lose your stability does not mean true believers can finally fall away. Peter has said they will never fall if they grow (1:10), and the warning is one of God’s means to keep them standing.

How do I actually grow in grace? Grace is the favour of God in Christ, known more deeply, and you grow in it through the means God has given: his word read, heard and preached; prayer; the Lord’s Supper and the fellowship of the church; and obedience, which opens the heart to know him more (John 14:21). Suffering and repentance help too, as each fresh sight of your need shows more of his kindness. Growth is slow and often unseen, like a tree’s; do not measure it day by day, but keep near the sources, and over years it will show.

3.theology:
The word of God and the uniform world: The scoffers claim that the world has always run on unchanged (v. 4). Peter points to two interruptions by the word of God, creation and the flood; the same word has spoken of a third, the fire.

Divine patience and salvation: Verse 9 says God is “not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.” How it stands with election is treated in the box “Where Christians differ: if God wishes all to repent, why are not all saved?” at v. 9.

New creation as promise: The new heavens and new earth of verse 13 are the goal toward which the whole letter looks. Herman Bavinck’s saying, grace restores nature (grace heals what God made; it does not replace it), applies here: the fire purifies creation rather than abolishing it, and the new creation is this creation glorified. Anthony Hoekema’s The Bible and the Future argues that the new earth is a renewal, not a replacement, which is why Christian hope is not escapism: the world we tend and serve matters, because it is the world God intends to redeem.
3.examples:
Then: The scoffers’ question, “Where is the promise of his coming?”, has been asked in every generation since the first believers died, and Peter’s answer stands: God’s patience is mercy.

Now: “What sort of people ought you to be” (v. 11) is the letter’s most searching question. A person who believes the day is coming lives with moral seriousness, urgency about the gospel, and longing for righteousness.

keyVerse.quote: The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.
keyVerse.note: This verse turns the scoffers’ argument inside out. The delay they offer as proof that nothing is coming is in fact proof of God’s mercy, the time he gives for repentance. It also explains every day the church has waited since, and Peter will turn it into a command: “count the patience of our Lord as salvation” (v. 15).

3.reflection:
The scoffers argued that because nothing seems to change, nothing will (v. 4), and Peter says their real motive was their own desires (v. 3). In what ways do we quietly live as though Christ were not coming? What does that show about our hearts?

Peter says the Lord’s delay is patience, “not wishing that any should perish” (v. 9). How does it change the way you see the long wait for Christ’s return, and the people you are praying for, to count each day as salvation (v. 15)?

Peter does not answer the end of the world with a timetable but with a question: “what sort of people ought you to be” (v. 11)? If this world is to be renewed, not discarded (v. 13), how should that shape your work, your money and your relationships this week?

Peter ends his last letter not by telling his readers to watch the heretics but to grow in the grace and knowledge of Christ (v. 18), and Paul and Peter, once at odds, are now “beloved brother” (v. 15). What do these verses show you about how grace changes a person, and where do you need to grow?
